d1 — distal demonstratives and adverbs

d1: distal demonstratives and adverbs

PropertyAnnotation
Primary familydeictic-a-i
Comparative input*a-t(u), *a-w-an/-ar; oblique *ad-an-i / *aw-an-i, *aw-att-i
Initial consonantØ
V1 quality / quantitya / short deictic input; secondary long formations
C2 identity / structuret/w/b / morphological dental/labial elements
Following vowela/i/u/variable
Root/formation shapedeictic base + gender/number + oblique augment
Grammatical categorypronoun/adverb
Boundary evidenceGender/number and oblique augments independently comparative; direct and oblique forms are distinct cells of one paradigm.
Input classpronominal-morphology
Telugu hypothesisoutside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule
Input confidencehigh for order and morphological augment; medium for exact immediate sequence
Overall confidencemedium
Eligibility / caveatmorphological-pronoun-domain

Independent input evidence. Tamil atu/avaṉ, Malayalam atu/avan, Kannada adu/ava and eastern ad/adi/avan establish a before the dental/labial. Tamil at-an-ai and Kannada ad-ar-ke independently establish a vowel-initial oblique augment (K03 p.222). This is morphological comparative evidence, not inference from Telugu dāni alone.

Direction. The same deictic a and proximal i precede gender/number elements throughout the family. Telugu and Konda apical/labial-initial obliques and masculine nominatives are innovative within that morphological alignment; they do not justify reconstructing initial d/v for the whole family.

Derivation and relative chronology. Proposed *ad-an-i > *daan-i > dāni; *aw-an-i > *waan-i > vāni, with modern plural vāṭi from a distinct *aw-att-i augment. Konda dani/vani can reflect subsequent shortening in obliques, but a directly contracted short outcome is not excluded. Telugu vā̃ḍu and Konda vānṟu require gender-formative history in addition to labial displacement. Konda abe/abeṇi : bān/bāṇi establishes a local labial-initial locative variant, with contraction and reformation not uniquely sequenced.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Count the distal and proximal entries as one deictic process family in the primary partition, not every inflected form as an independent root. Nominative adi and oblique dāni coexist by grammatical conditioning; simple claim all short V-apical words change is false. Labial participation is outside a narrowly apical lexical rule. K03 p.223 n.14 explicitly leaves shared Telugu–Konda innovation versus early Telugu borrowing unresolved. K03 p.222 n.13 proposes Old Telugu generalized the singular augment whereas spoken Telugu preserves *-att in the plural; this is a historical morphological hypothesis, not an independently dated sound change here. DEDR parser assigns obl broadly to whole paradigms and fragments Tamil forms/glosses; those tags are not all accurate POS analyses. Unrelated deictic compounds are preserved in full appendix but not counted as separate metatheses.

Mechanism scope. Morphologically restricted displacement/contraction plus analogy; labials participate.

Scholarly references. DEDR1; Krishnamurti2003 pp.158,222–223 nn.13–14

d61: shoot, discharge

C2 identity / structureṭ / singleton
Following vowela

Independent input evidence. Tulu aḍakuni and Telugu aḍarucu/aḍarincu agree in aḍa-, with different final extensions. The database PSTDr reconstruction rests on only this two-language comparison.

Direction. Both comparative members are vowel-initial; no independent displaced member motivates an earlier alternative order.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-a-r- > aḍarucu in Telugu; *aṭ-a-k- > aḍakuni in Tulu, conditionally on cognacy. No vowel/apical exchange is necessary.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. A low second vowel is directly shared, but the narrow distribution and final r:k mismatch limit the reconstruction level. The contrast is retained as a narrow comparison, not elevated to secure PDr evidence.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 61

d63 — hide, subdue, be compressed

d63: hide, subdue, be compressed

PropertyAnnotation
Primary familyd63
Comparative input*aṭ-a-nk- / *aṭ-a-nkk-
Initial consonantØ
V1 quality / quantitya / short
C2 identity / structureṭ / singleton
Following vowela
Root/formation shapeVC-a-NP / VC-a-NPP
Grammatical categoryverb
Boundary evidenceNasal intransitive versus stronger transitive formations recur independently in Tamil, Kannada, Telugu and the reconstruction.
Input classshort-vowel-initial-singleton-apical
Telugu hypothesiseligible; obligatory application predicts D
Input confidencehigh
Overall confidencehigh
Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭaŋku/aṭakku, Kannada aḍaŋgu/aḍaku and Telugu aḍãgu/aḍacu independently support the uncontracted low-vowel formative. K03 p.107 reconstructs these derivatives at Proto-South Dravidian level; PDr labels in CLDF are not precise historical levels.

Direction. The shared vowel-initial aṭ/aḍ order in SD I and aṛ- in Kurux–Malto, including the same stop/nasal formative contrasts, favors older *aṭ-aŋ- over an initial *ḍā- followed by multiple independent vowel insertions.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-aŋ- > *aḍ-aŋ- > *ḍāŋ- > Telugu ḍā̃gu/dā̃gu; independently *aṭ-aŋkk- > *ḍāŋc- > ḍā̃cu/dā̃cu. Literal *ḍaaŋ- contraction and assimilation/stress-induced V1 loss are competing implementations; the Telugu nasal-loss and initial ḍ>d are subsequent developments.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu retains aḍagu/aḍãgu “submit” and aḍacu “suppress” beside displaced “hide” forms: a real within-family semantic/formation split, not proof of a phonological exceptionless class. Kui also retains āṛpa/āṭpa. Kolami and Naikri are diagnosed as early Telugu loans by K03 p.107; aspiration in Naikri needs a recipient history. Tulu aḍeŋgɯ : ḍeŋgɯ/deŋguni is compatible with local aphaeresis, not independently the Telugu contraction. d80 shares compressed/piled semantics and homophonous Toda/Kannada evidence; sensitivity analysis should collapse d63+d80 without asserting that DEDR erred.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. K03 pp.107,162; PSS83 pp.229,233; K61 pp.51–54; DEDR 63

d64 — betel pouch

d64: betel pouch

PropertyAnnotation
Primary familyd64+d88
Comparative input*aṭ-a-ppay / *aṭay-ppay
Initial consonantØ
V1 quality / quantitya / short
C2 identity / structureṭ / singleton
Following vowela
Root/formation shapeVC-a(y) + pp-ay
Grammatical categorynoun
Boundary evidenceAreca + bag comparison is explicit in DEDR 88; probable cultural diffusion is not independently dated.
Input classshort-vowel-initial-singleton-apical
Telugu hypothesiseligible; obligatory application predicts D
Input confidencehigh
Overall confidencemedium
Eligibility / caveatcompound-contact-control

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭappam/aṭaippam, Malayalam aṭappam and Kannada aḍapa support aṭ-a-pp-. DEDR 88 supplies Tamil aṭaippai and explicitly cross-refers to this pouch family.

Direction. All daughter forms retain the vowel before ṭ/ḍ. Optional h in Kannada, Tulu and Telugu does not reverse the vowel/apical sequence.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭay-ppay (areca + bag) > aṭappam/aṭaippam and aḍapa-mu, with compounding and nominal-final alternation. The exact relation of pp-ay to -ppam needs separate morphology; no metathesis is needed.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Count together with d88, since the pouch is an areca compound and d88 actually repeats its Tamil form and Telugu derivatives. h-prothesis may mark regional transmission, but is not alone proof of a particular loan direction. This cultural vocabulary supplies an attested retention comparison with uncertain inheritance chronology.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭi, Kannada aḍi and Telugu aḍugu support *aṭ- and different vowel/consonant formatives. K03-derived CLDF reconstructions explicitly leave V unspecified.

Direction. Initial vowel preceding the apical occurs in SD I and Gondi–Konda, supporting V–C order without using Telugu as the sole conservative witness.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-Vk- > *aḍ-Vg- > Telugu aḍugu; Konda aḍgi shows medial-vowel loss without movement. Tamil/Kannada *aṭ-i gives aṭi/aḍi; they are not the identical -Vk derivative.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The independent suffix-vowel quality is not securely recovered: do not use Telugu u alone to prove a historical high-vowel class. Gadaba aḍugu is explicitly marked a Telugu loan. The Indo-Aryan heel forms attached to this family are contact comparisons, not votes for a Dravidian proto-vowel.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 72; K03 reconstruction records in Jambu

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭu (aṭuv-, aṭṭ-), Malayalam aṭuka and Kannada aḍu (aṭṭ-) support singleton *aṭ- and high-vowel verb formations independently of the geminate food noun *aṭṭu displayed at the DEDR head.

Direction. Both southern and south-central languages have vowel-initial roots, including Kui aṭa and Kuvi aṭ. An initial ṭ reconstruction would require unmotivated widespread prothesis.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-u- > retained cooking verbs; tense/noun strengthening yields aṭṭ- and Telugu aṭṭu. Telugu aḍugaṇṭu retains the singleton in a compound. Kui aṭa and Konda aṭk- retain order in heat/burn formations.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The pancake head is not the only reconstructed input of this etymon. Counting all members as geminate-root exclusions would discard eligible singleton derivatives. Conversely the geminate pancake alone does not test movement of a singleton. Telugu aḍasāla contains a separate kitchen component and may be regionally transmitted. Badaga aṭra/attara hot variants require local cluster/epenthesis history, not the initial metathesis examined here; nāgaṭṭte plant name has uncertain linkage.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 76; K03 pancake reconstruction in CLDF

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭu/aṭi/aṭar and Kannada aḍi/aḍar establish short a and postvocalic retroflex; Telugu aḍucu and aḍupu retain that ordering. Kui ḍāmba and Kuvi ḍamb- support a labial nasal formative but do not independently establish Telugu *-aŋ-.

Direction. Independent SD I vowel-initial forms plus Parji/Gadaba aṭ(t)- support earlier V–ṭ; deriving them all by vowel insertion before Proto-*ḍa- is poorly motivated.

Derivation and relative chronology. Possible *aṭ-aŋ- > *aḍ-aŋ- > *ḍāŋ- > ḍaŋgu > daŋgu, with shortening before NP; alternatively a consonantal formative produces short vowel directly. Transitive ḍancu/dancu and dampu have distinct extensions. Konda ḍaŋ-/ḍak-/ḍas- shows related displaced stems; exact shared suffixes require reconstruction.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Kui ā in ḍāmba supports investigating an early long vowel but is not an attested intermediate of Telugu ŋg. The Telugu non-displaced beat/fight forms must not be dropped. Tulu darpuni could reflect *aḍar- with aphaeresis, but the local vowel/stop history does not uniquely identify a literal swap. Kota ayṛ-/aṛc- is a distinct glide alternation.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭu, Malayalam aṭukka, Kannada aḍavu, Konda aṭ-, Pengo/Manda aḍ- support vowel-initial root. Telugu aḍaru has a different extension from the bare ability root.

Direction. Vowel-first root occurs in SD I, SD II and Malto, so the comparison supplies a broadly supported retained order.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-V- > aḍ-/aṭ- in daughter languages; Telugu *aḍ-ar- > aḍaru. Kui/Kuvi āḍ- lengthens while retaining V–C; this is not metathesis.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. A short-versus-long ability root alternation exists in Kuvi dialect/source records. Its quantity cannot be labeled concealed displacement because the apical remains postvocalic. Exact reconstruction of Telugu -ar- and whether it is productive morphology remain open.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭai and Kannada aḍe support *aṭ-ay- independently; Tamil/Kannada aṭu/aḍar and aḍapu show distinct extensions. Long and short Telugu outcomes cannot all be assigned one suffix.

Direction. SD I aṭ/aḍ-initial bases and Malto aṭg- preserve V–apical ordering; Telugu ḍā- and Kui ṛā- are innovations under the cognacy hypothesis.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-ay- > *aḍ-ay- > *ḍāy- > Telugu ḍāyu/dāyu; *aṭ-Vk- may yield *ḍak(k)- > ḍaggaṟa/daggaṟa, but the exact suffix and strengthening history are unresolved. Kui *aḍ-a-NC > ṛānja requires local ṭ/ṛ correspondence and is a separate derivation.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu aḍaru “arise” retains order; a derived -k- nearness noun differs from the -ay- approach verb. Kuvi dagira/daggire/ḍagre resembles the Telugu extended nearness word and may be a loan; independently proving that donor history is necessary before counting an inherited Kuvi innovation. Kui retains aḍa/aṭpa beside ṛānja etc. No semantic label is used as an automatic phonological condition.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. K61 vowel-initial cases pp.51–57; DEDR 79

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭukku, Malayalam aṭukkuka, Telugu aḍuku independently support high u in a pile formation; Kannada aḍuku/aḍaku and Kodagu aḍak-/aḍaŋg- show vowel and transitivity variants.

Direction. All attested branches keep the root vowel before the apical. The medial cluster in Nilgiri forms is a syncope outcome, not initial apical movement.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-ukk- > Tamil aṭukku; *aḍ-uk- > Telugu aḍuku; *aḍ-Vk- > Kota aṛk-/Toda oṛk-. No displacement is required for any reviewed reflex.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This is a retained high-formative counterpart to displaced high-formative cases elsewhere: vowel height alone does not decide application. The etymon overlaps d63 in Toda oṛk- “subdue, pile” and Kannada packing vocabulary. Report both strict DEDR counts and a conservative collapse with d63; do not count the same Toda token twice as independent root evidence.

Independent input evidence. Telugu aḍugu and Parji aḍ-/aḍi support older vowel–apical order; Tamil aḷavu has a lateral and Tulu naṭṭu adds n and gemination. The precise PDr reconstruction is less secure than its starred CLDF display suggests.

Direction. Vowel-first Telugu and Parji agree, while Kui jāpa is analyzed in DEDR as an innovative reflex with a special ṭ : j correspondence. The disparate Tamil/Tulu roots prevent simply assuming all strings are regular descendants of one fully specified stem.

Derivation and relative chronology. Telugu *aḍ-ug- > aḍugu retains order. Under DEDR cognacy, Kui *aṭ-a-p- > *ṭāp- > jāp- is a possible displacement derivation, requiring a low formative distinct from Telugu u and independent support for ṭ>j.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. DEDR cites Burrow and Bhattacharya, IIJ 5:122 for ṭ : Kui j; that primary argument has not yet been obtained. The Kui history remains tentative, not a secure success in a quantitative sound-law test. Tamil lateral and Tulu n require either separate changes, morphological analysis, or revised cognacy.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭai and Malayalam aṭayuka support singleton *aṭ-ay, while Tamil aṭṭam, Kannada aḍḍa and Telugu aḍḍamu independently support a strengthened transverse/obstruction formation. Both must be represented.

Direction. Numerous SD I and SD II forms retain initial a. Initial ḍ in Kui ḍākoli could be displaced, but the word is not segmentally identical to the native simple closing stems and needs independent history.

Derivation and relative chronology. Retained *aṭay > Tamil aṭai / Tulu aḍe-vuni; strengthened *aṭṭa > Telugu aḍḍa(mu). Telugu aḍucu-konu retains the singleton in a derived construction. Hypothetical *aṭ-a-k... > *ḍāk... for Kui shield remains unverified.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not classify the entire etymon as a geminate blocker from Telugu aḍḍa alone. Kui aḍa is explicitly said to be from Oriya; ḍākoli shield could be inherited, compounded or borrowed, with no independently recovered complete input. Brahui āṛ and Malto aṛatre have explicit IA doubts. The broad IA obstruction series is contact evidence, not extra independent Dravidian controls. Kuvi kīnai is an extracted light verb, not a standalone cognate of aṭ-.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭai/aṭar, Kannada aḍe/aḍar and Telugu aḍaru establish short a, singleton apical and low vowel extensions. These are independent of the strengthened pile nouns.

Direction. SD I, Telugu, Konda aḍar and Pengo aḍer all put a before the apical; no reversal is required.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-ar- > aḍaru in Telugu and aḍar in Kannada/Konda. *aṭ-ay- > aṭai/aḍe; strengthened *aṭṭ- appears in pile nouns. Pengo e after the apical is a local vowel development without displacement.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu eṭṭam differs in V1, and aṭṭaḍi/aṭṭava have strengthened compound-like shapes: these are not examples of initial displacement. The root is semantically close to pile d80 and approach d79; audit an alternative broad family collapse rather than treating semantic similarity as proof of one root.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭai “support” and aṭai-kal “anvil”, Malayalam aṭa-kkallu and Kannada aḍe-gal/aḍa-gallu establish the support-stone compound independently of Telugu.

Direction. Vowel-first support nouns in three southern languages and Kota aṛ gal favor original *aṭay; Telugu initial ḍā is an innovation in the first compound member.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭ-ay-kal > *aḍ-ay-kal > *ḍāy-kal > ḍā-kallu / ḍā-kali > dākali; dāyi can reflect the uncompounded first member. Intermediate y loss and changes of the stone component are separate from displacement.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This compound shows that a morphological boundary after the eligible first member need not block displacement. It does not license moving arbitrary consonants across a compound boundary. The detailed kali/gali/kallu variation needs suffix/compound history; it is not a free phonological substitution. No independent SCDr non-Telugu attestation is in this set.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 86; K61 vowel-initial displacement pp.51–57

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṭaikkāy, Malayalam aṭakka/aṭekka and Kannada aḍake support the areca + fruit compound; Kannada aḍa and tool compounds support a reduced first member independently.

Direction. Vowel-first ordering is supported by several SD I languages. Koraga initial ḍ can arise by loss of initial a in a locally contracted areca word, without importing a Telugu history.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṭay-kkāy > aṭaikkāy / aḍake, then in Tappu Koraga *aḍakke > ḍakke by aphaeresis and local compound reduction. Telugu aḍa-katti etc. retain the first member; aḍḍa-kattera has additional strengthening.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Koraga preserves short a after the initial stop and a following geminate, so this is compatible with straightforward aphaeresis; a literal vowel/stop exchange is not demonstrated. Telugu has tools/bag attendants, not the identical inherited fruit noun; contact among areca-using communities remains plausible. Kannada Areca catecʰu is a botanical Latin fragment misparsed as a Kannada form and is excluded. Count d64+d88 once as the areca/bag family.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 88,64; K03 SD I areca reconstruction

Independent input evidence. Kannada nīr-aṛ̆ke/nīr-aḍike, Kolami aḍḍ-, Naikri aḍ and Parji/Gadaba anḍ suggest a vowel-initial apical base, but disagree on apical identity and pre-apical nasal/gemination. Starostin marks the reconstruction questionable.

Direction. All non-Telugu comparanda favor a before an apical; Telugu ḍappi could be displaced if the comparison is correct. Their divergent consonants prevent a unique detailed proto-form.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *aḍ-p- > *ḍa-pp- > ḍappi > dappi, with formative strengthening, is compatible with the short vowel. An older nasal or *ẓ requires different consonant developments. No *aḍa- input is inserted just to predict ā and then explain it away.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This is evidence for investigating displacement, but not a secure geminate exception or proof of a low-vowel shortening rule. Kannada aṛ̆ is a distinct historical apical, while Parji/Gadaba have a nasal. Etymon d277 also contains ḍappi in the sense distress/perishing: evaluate lexical conflation and possible semantic overlap. A primary source paradigm for thirst dayyu and an early dated ḍappi would help separate analyses.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. DEDR explicitly derives the family from Sanskrit rājan-. K03 pp.476–477 independently identifies Tamil aracan and Kannada arasu as early adapted loans with prothetic a. Toda source explicitly says Kannada/Sanskrit borrowing.

Direction. Comparative direction is donor r-initial > recipient ar-initial, not Proto-Dravidian ar- > r-. Modern initial a in several Dravidian languages therefore does not establish inherited a-r ordering.

Derivation and relative chronology. Sanskrit rājan- > regional *arāca- > araca(n)/arasu/arusu, with prothesis, quantity adaptation, intervocalic consonant adaptation and recipient endings. Intermediate recipient steps are schematic; a single shared borrowing episode is not established.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The PSTDr starred database head is a regional comparison, not evidence that this is inherited PDr. Telugu rāju elsewhere is not automatically a metathesized doublet of arusu: separate Sanskrit loan strata must be tested. DEDR cites a 2nd-century Śātavāhana coin form arahaṇasha, but identifies its language as unknown and only presumably South Dravidian; it cannot securely date specifically Telugu metathesis.

Mechanism scope. Prothesis and loan adaptation, not inherited apical displacement

Scholarly references. DEDR 201 editorial note; K03 pp.476–478; Sircar 1961 EI 35:247–252 cited by DEDR (not independently checked)

Independent input evidence. Tamil aracu/arai, Malayalam aracu/arayāl and Kannada arase/araḷi support initial ar-a- and several lexical extensions. K03 p.10 lists *ar-ac/-aḷ; those are not literal ancestors of Telugu rāvi.

Direction. Several SD I languages retain ar- and show internal suffix variation. The parsimonious directional comparison is ar-a- > rā-, but it does not independently reconstruct the final Telugu consonant.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ar-a-... > *rā-... > rāvi/rāgi, with the -v/-g material unexplained by displacement itself. A specific *ar-avi or *ar-agi intermediate would be a fitted reconstruction and is not asserted.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Kannada rāvi is explicitly borrowed from Telugu. Kolami ra·vi and Konda rāyi maran could reflect contact with Telugu tree terminology; no independent chronology establishes separate innovations. Tamil arai already has a reduced extension, so later truncation is possible but does not explain all v/g/y correspondences.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. K03 p.10; DEDR 202

Independent input evidence. Telugu araṭi/araṇṭi/arãṭi and anaṇṭi/anãṭi/aṇṭi provide internal variation. The only non-Telugu evidence, Gondi arṭi, is explicitly marked borrowed from Telugu; K03 labels the reconstruction SD II, but the current set does not independently justify a shared proto-stage.

Direction. Telugu variants favor an older r-containing local stem, but no independent inherited cognate establishes exact early segment order or V2. The Gondi loan reproduces recipient syncope after borrowing.

Derivation and relative chronology. Within the local family araṇṭi > arãṭi/araṭi is compatible with nasal weakening/loss; araṇṭi > anaṇṭi suggests regressive nasal assimilation; reduction gives aṇṭi. Relative order of these reductions is not uniquely recoverable.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. No initial *rā- reflex occurs, and the loss of r in aṇṭi does not require concealed metathesis. Treat as a single-language reconstruction problem, not an independently reconstructed unchanged success. The Kittel-only variants may preserve valuable dialect history; independent historical spellings could decide the r/n chronology.

Mechanism scope. Nasal assimilation, nasal loss and stem reduction; no displacement demonstrated

Scholarly references. DEDR 205; K03 SD II reconstruction in CLDF

Independent input evidence. Tamil aril and Telugu aralu independently provide initial ar- plus a later lateral. Telugu allu and Salur Gadaba all lack the rhotic. Tamil i versus Telugu a prevents recovering one exact medial vowel.

Direction. The rhotic-bearing Tamil and Telugu forms favor an earlier ar-V-l sequence; rhotic assimilation after medial syncope produces ll more economically than a vowel–rhotic swap followed by reinsertion of initial a.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ar-V-l- > *ar-l- > *al-l- > Telugu allu, Gadaba all, conditional on cognacy. Telugu aralu retains the longer formation. This orders vowel loss before rl assimilation, but does not independently date either.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The lexeme may be related to weaving d260; evaluate a merged family sensitivity because allu occurs in both with closely related senses. The r-bearing witnesses prevent automatically treating every all- as original geminate l. Whether Gadaba borrowed Telugu allu rather than inherited the assimilation remains open.

Mechanism scope. Medial syncope and rhotic–lateral assimilation; not initial displacement

Scholarly references. DEDR 207; compare DEDR 260

Independent input evidence. Tamil arai trunk and Kannada araḷe post independently support initial ar- and low vowel; Telugu rāḍu and Kolami rāḍ/rāl have different final consonants. The database initial *rāḍ head is not automatically the earlier comparative input.

Direction. A low-vowel *ara- regional input is favored by the Tamil/Kannada comparison and the broader displacement correspondence, but the final y/ḷ/ḍ variation weakens a fully specified reconstruction.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *ar-aḌ > *rāḌ > Telugu rāḍu, or *aray plus a later ḍ-bearing nominal formation. The exact final consonant and morphological sequence remain unknown. Gondi rāyi and Kolami rāḍ/rāl may share the innovation or be loans from Telugu.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not reconstruct final *ḍ solely because Telugu has it. Trunk/post/peg semantics are compatible, but culture-word diffusion is a real competing explanation for the regional r-initial forms. A dated donor form, a wider pattern of Kolami ḍ/l variation, or a matching southern ḍ-bearing derivative would discriminate.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil ari/arici, Malayalam ari and Tulu ari/argi independently attest vowel-first r. Kannada/Kodagu akki and Kota/Toda forms require medial cluster histories; Telugu arise is a rice-food derivative.

Direction. Bare ari and cluster-bearing argi favor earlier V–r order, making akki explainable by medial assimilation rather than apical promotion.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *ar-ki > *arki > akki in Kannada/Kodagu, beside preserved Tulu argi; Tamil arici has a palatal formation or different development. Telugu arise retains ar-; mapping its s directly onto the whole arici formation remains a hypothesis requiring source history.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Rice terminology has a wider contact history, but this entry alone does not decide ultimate origin. Telugu attests a particular food name, not the basic rice word: late culinary borrowing could make it ineligible for an inherited sound law. Toda nel-compounds and Badaga dish names are derivatives, not additional roots. A Tulu bibliographic fragment is not a lexical record.

Mechanism scope. Retention and medial assimilation; exact velar/palatal formation history unresolved

Scholarly references. DEDR 215; comparative origin beyond the regional input unresolved

Independent input evidence. Tamil ari and Telugu ari agree in the tax noun; Telugu aruvu supplies another rhotic formation. The relationship of Kannada/Telugu accu and Telugu appu to these nouns is not a regular consequence of metathesis.

Direction. Vowel-first ari is independently supported, but it does not alone reconstruct the entire debt series. A hypothetical *ar-pp > appu requires assimilation and a separately motivated formative, not initial-r movement.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ari > retained tax noun. Conditional *ar-pp- > *app- > appu and *ar-cc- > *acc- > accu invoke regressive assimilation or loss of the rhotic after suffix combination. Their exact formative origins are unresolved. No initial *rV- stage is necessary.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. DEDR cross-refers to d223 arukku take, snatch, demand; that may explain the payment verb semantically, but must be reviewed before a single derivation is accepted. Tamil appu and Kuvi aruvu/aṛvū are explicit Telugu loans. They do not independently corroborate a common *ar-pp stage.

Mechanism scope. Possible suffix-triggered cluster assimilation, not evidence for apical displacement

Scholarly references. DEDR 216 and cross-reference to 223

Independent input evidence. Tamil aru/ariya, Malayalam arutu/ariya and Kannada arudu/aridu independently support a short ar- base with high-vowel extensions. Telugu arudu/aridi preserves both qualities.

Direction. All reviewed languages place a before r; there is no evidence for earlier initial r followed by inserted a.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ar-u-tu > arudu in Telugu/Kannada, beside *ar-i- formations; Kota arg-/Toda arx- show ordinary loss of a medial high vowel. No displacement is required.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The bare root may be free, but the -t- nominal/adjectival formation is independently comparable and supplies a retained formative-bearing control. Tamil long āri etc. are root-quantity variants, not inferred metathesis stages. Kota “cry out in pain” appears as a separate lexicographic sense and is not used to reconstruct this family.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aruku/aruvu, Malayalam ariku/aruvu and Kannada arugu/arigu independently show short ar- and high-vowel extensions; Telugu arugu and aṟu/aṟuta have rhotic spelling variation.

Direction. Multiple southern languages place the root vowel before r. Telugu agrees; no displacement or restoration of an earlier displaced form is demanded.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ar-uk- > aruku/arugu; *ar-uv- > aruvu; short base *ar-u > aṟu and related locative/adverbial extensions. Telugu arudencu contains additional come/go morphology rather than a reversed root.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Kannada aragu has a low-vowel variant, and Gondi araluk is a more extended close/follow expression; neither can be used to assign the same historical V2 to all forms. Kurux arbar-parbar is a paired/echo expression with uncertain exact cognacy. Telugu ṟ/r history needs early spellings, but both preserve vowel-first order.

Independent input evidence. Tamil aruḷ, Malayalam aruḷ and Telugu arulu independently support the two-liquid stem, with Telugu merger of retroflex lateral. Kota arḷ has medial vowel loss.

Direction. The ordering ar-u-ḷ is common to the southern and Telugu evidence; Kota syncope supports loss of the medial vowel rather than a shift of the rhotic to the start.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aruḷ > Telugu arulu, with ḷ>l; *aruḷ > Kota arḷ by syncope. Neither change requires metathesis. Date and direction of possible religious vocabulary transmission are unknown.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The source compares d381 ārvam and tentatively d203 araṇa; neither proves a productive -uḷ formative. Treat this as an eligible root-shape comparison with uncertain morphological status, not an invented free-root exception. Affection and divine utterance differ semantically but have ordinary potential links through favor/command.

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil arai, Malayalam arayuka and Kannada are/arayisu establish the ar-ay type independently. Telugu ṟ/r doublets need historical rhotic checking; their existence does not overturn the cross-language V–rhotic ordering.

Direction. The wide SD I ar- comparison and Gondi aṛs make vowel-first order preferable; Telugu rā- and several SCDr r-initial formations are innovative. The initial vowel cannot be restored merely from a hypothesized ban on initial r.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ar-ay- > *rāy- > Telugu rāyu; strengthened/transitive derivatives give rācu/ṟācu and rāpu/ṟāpu. Different rē-/re- formations in Konda, Kui and Pengo require a vowel or suffix history beyond simple a+a contraction. Kui rāk-p- > rāpka illustrates separate stop metathesis after the initial displacement.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu fragment nouns aravuḍu/aṟavaṟalu preserve order; ragulu/ravulu “kindle” have short a and semantic drift, so no unique long-to-short derivation is assumed. Kuvi mlekʰ'nai lacks a convincing segmental path from ar- and remains a questionable member. Gondi Koya rāy may be influenced by Telugu; Kolami rāk is a loan candidate. Malayalam rākuka beside irāvuka could arise by local aphaeresis plus v/k derivational variation. Neither southern nor central initial r automatically demonstrates shared inheritance.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 228; PSS83 pp.246–248 on independent southern aphaeresis

Independent input evidence. Tamil arai, Kannada are, Telugu ara/aṟa and Naiki ar establish V–r ordering and the ay/a/e regional vowel correspondences.

Direction. The same ordering is widespread within SD I and retained in Telugu and Naiki. Nothing requires either a prior displacement or reinsertion.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aray > Tamil arai, Kannada/Tulu are, Malayalam/Telugu ara; Kota/Toda/Naiki ar lose the final vowel. These changes do not relocate the rhotic.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This is a useful contrast to *ar-ay “grind”, but historical identity of the formative -ay is not proven: half may be a lexical free base, whereas grind enters verbal derivation. The distinction cannot be manufactured after noticing opposite outcomes. Telugu ṟ/r is recorded but its chronology remains unestablished.

Independent input evidence. Kota and Toda arb have r before b; Telugu abbu and Kuvi abbinai have a geminate b and compatible enjoyment/prosperity semantics. The shared Nilgiri form is not independent evidence for a particular lost vowel.

Direction. If cognate, arb > abb by assimilation is preferable to reconstructing initial r and then losing it while restoring a. The current evidence does not determine whether rb was original or produced by syncope.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ar(V)b- > *arb- > abb- > Telugu abbu, conditionally on cognacy. Kuvi abb- may share assimilation or be influenced by Telugu. No initial apical displacement is needed.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The reconstructed boundary and vowels are unknown; label this a probable competing mechanism, not a regular retained liquid outcome. Nilgiri extreme happiness versus Telugu acquire/Kuvi prosper is semantically plausible but not proof. An uncontracted matching derivative outside Nilgiri or early Kuvi evidence would strengthen the comparison.

Mechanism scope. Probable rb assimilation, with syncope optional and cognacy provisional

Independent input evidence. Gondi ar, Konda ar/arap and Pengo ar- support the vowel-first root. The -al required by Telugu rālu is not independently preserved in this current DEDR set; K61 p.56 compares Tamil aṟ-al, outside the present grouping.

Direction. Regional ar- stems independently favor earlier V–r order. Telugu rāl- has an added lateral formation; the Koya rāl loan cannot be counted as independent support for its antiquity.

Derivation and relative chronology. If the older -al comparison is accepted, *ar-al- > *rāl- > Telugu rālu, with causative rāl-p-/rāl-c-. Pengo ar- : rat- suggests displacement in a derived causative. Kuvi rī- and Manda re- cannot be predicted from *ar-al; their formations and vowel histories remain separate.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Gondi rāl is explicitly labeled from Telugu. Kolami/Naikri rāl- forms are probable contact comparanda but have not been independently dated. K61 source comparison must be checked before *ar-al is treated as a secure low-vowel input. A shared abstract “fall” meaning does not make every derivative identical.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. K61 p.56; PSS83 p.233; DEDR 233

Independent input evidence. Tamil alai/alaŋku, Malayalam alayuka/alaŋŋuka, Telugu alayu/alãgu independently supply short al-a- and extended stems. The CLDF negative *al “be not” is not evidence for this lexical family.

Direction. SD I, Telugu, Kolami and Parji agree on initial al-; r/l-initial variants need their own histories rather than a uniform reconstructed initial liquid.

Derivation and relative chronology. Retained *al-a-y > Telugu alayu and *al-aŋ- > alãgu. Telugu lampaṭa and Kannada lampaṭe admit initial-vowel loss or contact-related restructuring; their exact earlier compound is unknown. Kui laha may reflect loss/reordering from al-a-, but short a and h are not fully explained.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. DEDR explicitly separates Sanskrit-derived Telugu lampaṭũḍu from the trouble noun and tentatively proposes Dravidian > Sanskrit borrowing for lampaṭa. This can involve export and reborrowing, not a simple one-way loan label. Kurux layā- vs algā requires separate suffix and vowel analysis. A bogus Malto alaŋku row is actually the opening of DEDR editorial prose about Tamil; only Malto alesi is lexical evidence. DEDR warns that d236 “suffer” and d240 “move” have converged semantically; separate roots remain the primary partition, with a collapsed sensitivity analysis.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 236 and preserved editorial comparison; PSS83 pp.246–248

Independent input evidence. Tamil alai/alaŋku, Malayalam alayuka/alaŋŋuka and Kannada ale/alagu supply medial l and low formative independently; Telugu ala and allāḍu preserve the order.

Direction. The shared vowel-first SD I/Telugu base plus Kurux alr- favors original al-. Kui lāng- is a derived innovative outcome, not a reason to reverse the reconstructed comparison.

Derivation and relative chronology. *al-aŋ- > *lāŋ- > Kui lānga; its causative lāk-p- > lāpka requires separate stop-cluster metathesis. Telugu allāḍu can be analyzed as a reinforced/reduplicated formation associated with “move” and must not be reduced to an imaginary initial *lā-. Pengo lem- and Irula le·- require a separate vowel and derivative history.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Tulu landuni/landele may show independent aphaeresis in a wanderer derivative; no shared SCDr event follows. Pengo e and Irula e· cannot be generated by simple a+a contraction without another change. Malayalam alaŋŋ-/anaŋŋ- is l/n assimilation/variation, not vowel–liquid displacement. DEDR treats this root as originally distinct from d236 but acknowledges semantic convergence.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 240; DEDR 236 editorial note

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam alaŋkōlam and Kannada/Telugu allakallōla share a complex stem. DEDR compares both shake alaŋku d240 and Sanskrit kallola wave; this is not secure evidence for a uniform simple proto-root.

Direction. All forms preserve initial a. The mixed shape can reflect lexical remodeling or a compound/echo formation rather than any displacement of the initial lateral.

Derivation and relative chronology. A shake-root formation associated with alaŋku may have converged with kallola wave; gemination and the repeated all-/kall- shape require lexical/morphological history. The evidence does not uniquely order those developments.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Exclude this opaque complex formation from the decisive singleton-root denominator. It remains relevant to how analogy/borrowing can create apparent controls. Tulu allambra has a different final cluster and cannot be generated by simply swapping a and l.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Malayalam alaśaṇṭa/alasāndram, Kannada alasande and Telugu alacandalu support a regional vowel-first crop name. DEDR compares Prakrit ālisaṃdaga/ālisaṃdaya and Marathi aḷasudā, so deep Dravidian inheritance is not established.

Direction. Tulu brahmin alasaṇḍɛ and non-brahmin lattaṇḍɛ/lattanɛ supply a source-labeled initial-loss contrast. Other Dravidian forms agree on initial a, but this does not settle the ultimate loan direction.

Derivation and relative chronology. Tulu alasaṇḍ- > alataṇḍ- (attested B-K variant) > lattaṇḍ-/lattan- is an illustrative sequence of s/t change, initial loss, strengthening and cluster simplification; exact ordering and variant ancestry are not proven. Telugu alacand-/alasand- keeps initial al-.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Five Kannada forms were misassigned Malayalam by the parser; corrected only in research. Botanical Latin is excluded. Tulu sociolinguistic labels are preserved and not assumed to represent successive historical periods. An inherited sound-law denominator would require an independently dated Dravidian entry of the crop name, so this is a contact/lexical control.

Mechanism scope. Regional lexical diffusion and local aphaeresis/assimilation candidate

Scholarly references. DEDR 242 p.23, original language headings inspected; B-K/Männer/BRR source labels

Independent input evidence. Kannada alabu/alubu and Telugu alamu agree on vowel-first al-, but b:m and a:u variation do not uniquely support the full starred *alamb- supplied in CLDF. Gondi allam is explicitly a Telugu loan.

Direction. The two non-identical comparison stems both preserve a before l. There is no displaced form from which an earlier reversed order can be independently inferred.

Derivation and relative chronology. A regional *al-Vmb- could yield Kannada alabu and Telugu alamu by different cluster reductions, but neither the nasal cluster nor a common V2 is securely attested. No metathesis is required.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Botanical identifications and semantic breadth need primary lexicographic checking. The Kannada Latin genus record Alysicarpus is a parsing artifact. This narrow comparison is useful for recording uncertainty, not for proving a PDr unchanged control.

Independent input evidence. Tamil alappu/alampu/alaṟu, Malayalam alappu/alaṟuka and Old Kannada alaṟu support a low-vowel initial al-a- base independently. Telugu has different alikiḍi/alabalamu formations.

Direction. Independent southern arousal/noise stems support a before l; Irula lā·ru is plausibly an innovative initial-loss/contraction outcome of the roaring derivative.

Derivation and relative chronology. *al-aṟ- > alaṟu in Tamil/Old Kannada; possible *alaṟ- > *lāṟ- > Irula lā·ru. This could involve vowel coalescence with apical displacement or aphaeresis and compensatory lengthening. Telugu alikiḍi has a high-vowel extension not identical to the roaring stem.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not group by expressive meaning to exempt words from sound change: the morphological and segmental inputs still need reconstruction. Malayalam aḷavan boaster is explicitly an alternative comparison with measure d296, so retroflex ḷ is not silently regularized to l. Irula length and donor/native status require a local source history before counting a shared SCDr innovation.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil alaicu/alampu, Malayalam alakkuka/alampuka and Kannada ale/alambu independently support vowel-first al- and low-vowel formations. Kannada alumbu and Telugu aluku supply high-vowel variants.

Direction. Southern cognates favor earlier initial al-. Tulu lumbuni can be derived directly from the attested alumbuni by aphaeresis; Kui akali requires a different account of k and l positions.

Derivation and relative chronology. *al-amp- > retained alamp-/alamb-; *al-ump- > Tulu alumbuni > lumbuni by initial a loss. Telugu alãdu and aluku have separate consonantal extensions. Conditional *al-akk- > *ak-al- > Kui akali would be nonadjacent consonant transposition, but the exact input/formation is not independently established.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Tulu retains u after l and a nasal cluster, so an initial vowel/stop exchange is unnecessary. Kui akali is genuinely printed in a Kui vocabulary, with akali-pakali and light-verb constructions; it is not merely a Jambu typo. The existence of that noun does not prove its DEDR etymology. Toda as̱p- lacks l and may involve a local lateral-plus-stop development; its exact history must be checked separately.

Mechanism scope. Retentions plus independent aphaeresis; possible other consonant metathesis in Kui

Scholarly references. DEDR 246; Winfield 1929, A Vocabulary of the Kui Language, p.3; NBU handle 123456789/1942 (title and entry visually checked)

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil alar, Malayalam alar and Telugu alaru support older l...r order, independently of Kannada/Tulu variants. Kannada retains alar beside aral/araḷ, so both orders occur within one language.

Direction. Concordant l...r in Tamil, Malayalam and Telugu plus retained Kannada alar favors *alar > aral, not *aral as the uniform family input. There is no evidence that the initial vowel has moved.

Derivation and relative chronology. *alar > Kannada/Tulu aral by nonadjacent consonant metathesis; *aral > araḷ by a separate lateral change. Kannada alal may instead reflect r-to-l assimilation. Kannada arlu involves medial syncope, plausibly after the r...l ordering had developed.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This is a real comparative metathesis candidate outside Telugu, but a different process from initial apical promotion. R in the main outcome matrix means the target initial V–apical order remains; an orthogonal process annotation records the l/r exchange. DEDR tentatively relates beauty d248, which must be collapsed in a conservative family sensitivity. Marathi araḷ/arala is a contact comparison, not an independent Dravidian language vote.

Mechanism scope. Nonadjacent l...r > r...l metathesis in Kannada/Tulu; no initial-vowel displacement

Scholarly references. DEDR 247 and editorial cross-references to DEDR 248 and Marathi

Direction. Vowel-first ordering is supported by the Tamil/Telugu comparison and by Kannada alampu itself. The lampu variant is therefore an innovation, without requiring a displaced shared proto-root.

Direction. The current evidence gives only a local vowel-first stem, not a comparative proof of a Proto-South-Central *ala-. The database starred PSD2 root overstates what this isolated group can establish.

Derivation and relative chronology. Telugu ala-vaḍu : ala-vaṟucu : ala-vāṭu exhibits verb/causative/nominal morphology. No initial consonant movement is observed; chronology and origin of the first component are unknown.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This cannot become a secure retained sound-law counterexample merely because it looks like ala-. Conversely, absence of independent cognates does not prove it entered Telugu too late for the sound change. A dated early compound and independently cognate first member would resolve eligibility.

Independent input evidence. Tamil, Malayalam, Tulu and Telugu independently attest alli with ll. The singleton *ali reconstruction displayed in an imported record is not supported by a singleton reflex in this comparison.

Direction. The four-language agreement favors earlier geminate ll for the shared lexical input; there is no reason to delete one l merely to place this root in the metathesis-eligible class.

Derivation and relative chronology. *alli > alli across the reviewed languages; Tulu allige adds a nominal extension. No apical promotion occurs.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Tamil pulli is explicitly contrasted stamen vocabulary, not another reflex of alli; the Latin plant name is a gloss, not a Tamil form. Ultimate plant-name borrowing cannot be excluded, but the independent gemination makes this a useful structural control without relying on outcome.

Direction. All languages retain an initial vowel before l. Compound forms establish singleton evidence independently, without implying that bare and compounded variants had identical historical shapes.

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṛ̆al and Malayalam aṛ̆aluka support *aẓ-al independently; Tamil aṛ̆uŋku supports a different high-vowel nasal extension. Old Kannada aṛ̆v and Tulu arluni corroborate the vowel-first root. The database head **aẓVnkV is not the sole reconstructed formation.

Direction. The southern comparison favors V–ẓ order for the regional input. DEDR tentatively connects initial t-bearing fire vocabulary d3115: that would place earlier initial-consonant loss before the regional vowel-initial stage, but is not established by this set alone.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aẓ-al > Telugu aḍalu/aḍaru with ẓ>ḍ and final-liquid variation, without initial displacement. Kannada aẓ-kaj > akkaja illustrates cluster assimilation. Conditional *aẓ-V-mp > *ẓV̄mp > Konda ṛīmbu would require an independently justified high-vowel history; the modern ī is not sufficient to reconstruct that history.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Konda ember and Kuvi blaze/light forms begin ṛī-, compatible with displacement but with unexplained vowel quality and different extensions. Gondi eṛki/eṛk explicitly carries DEDR’s warning that its vowel is difficult. Kota arl fever has an alternative d214 comparison. Tamil aṭalai and Kannada aḍalu/aṛ̆al are source-marked Telugu loans. Kurux aŋgnā may lose ẓ in a medial cluster; it is not evidence of initial relocation.

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṛ̆i with transitive -pp-/-tt-, Malayalam aṛ̆iyuka/aṛ̆ikka and Kannada aṛ̆i/aṛ̆ipu independently support high i and vowel-first ẓ. K03 p.195 explicitly derives Telugu destruction forms from non-past *aẓ-i-mpp and past *aẓ-i-ntt.

Direction. SD I and Gondi vowel-first stems, together with retained Telugu aṛ̆isina/aṛ̆ipuṭa, favor earlier aẓi-. Inscriptional Telugu ṛ̆accu has initial ẓ while still preserving its identity: displacement need not wait until ẓ has become ḍ.

Derivation and relative chronology. K03: *aẓ-i-ntt > *aẓ-i-cc > inscriptional ẓaccu; *aẓ-i-mpp > *ẓapp- > Telugu ḍappi. Palatalization after i must precede deletion of its conditioning vowel under this account. Initial ẓ>ḍ follows displacement in the labial formation; the inscriptional palatal formation directly attests the otherwise hidden initial-ẓ stage. These are related tense/voice formations, not two independent sound-change events.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Sastri 1969 pp.310–311, inscription38 (dated there 890 CE), has displaced ḻassi line14 and retained aḻisina lines20–21, aḻiputa line35 in one text, but different grammatical formations: coexistence is not identical-context free variation. Earlier inscription16 (pp.291–292, dated 670–680) has ḻaccina; DHARMA00026 distinguishes this reading from older editorial ḍaccina. ṛ̆assi and ḍappi are displaced, but ḍakkā has a different extension and remains uncertain. Parji/Gadaba killing forms have an explicit alternative d309. Homophonous thirst ḍappi d109 must not be merged solely by spelling.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. K03 pp.194–195; DEDR 277; Sastri 1969 pp.291–292 inscription16, pp.310–311 inscription38, p.350 index; https://dharmalekha.info/texts/INSTelugu00026

Independent input evidence. Malayalam aṛ̆ivu and Kannada aṛ̆ipu independently support vowel-first *aẓi; Kannada aṛ̆kaṟ beside akkaṟe directly supplies the relevant medial-cluster comparison.

Direction. Kannada preserves both ẓk and kk, favoring assimilation after medial syncope. Telugu akkaṟa remains vowel-initial, so its missing ẓ does not require an earlier initial promotion.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aẓi-kar > *aẓkar > akkar gives Telugu akkaṟa and Kannada akkaṟe with regressive assimilation ẓk>kk. *aẓ-ti > arti retains the rhotic-order reflex in another formation; remaining suffix vowels vary independently.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. DEDR tentatively relates burn/grieve d276, so root independence needs a sensitivity collapse. Tulu arti has an alternative long-root d381 comparison. Toda arkyn and Kota akm have different final morphology; their exact full derivations are less secure than the initial-order diagnosis.

Mechanism scope. Medial syncope and regressive consonant assimilation, not initial apical displacement

Scholarly references. DEDR 281 and cross-references d276,381

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṛ̆u/aṛ̆ai, Malayalam aṛ̆uka, Kannada aṛ̆u and Gondi–Konda aṛ- independently establish vowel-first apical and at least u/ay formations. PSS83 pp.14–15 compares *aẓ-u; the database Starostin *jeẓ head is an alternative analysis, not adopted as a given.

Direction. Agreement of SD I, Gondi–Konda, Central Dravidian and retained Pengo aṛ- favors earlier V–ẓ. Kui/Kuvi/Manda initial ṛ are innovative under this cognacy, but their ī needs a regional vowel explanation. Pengo causatives supply a within-language original/displaced contrast.

Derivation and relative chronology. Retained *aẓ-u > Telugu ēḍu- requires vowel fronting/lengthening before or alongside ẓ>ḍ; ēḍucu has an incorporated past palatal according to K03 p.193. Pengo aṛ-/aṛba versus ṛat/ṛatpa shows apical displacement in causative formations; a possible *aẓ-a-t > ṛat route remains conditional. Kui/Kuvi/Manda *aẓV > ṛī is directionally plausible, but a uniquely supported sequence yielding ī is not yet available.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu long ē does not mean metathesis: the apical is still after the vowel. Pengo ṛatpa is a source correction of earlier aratpa, which would reverse its outcome classification if not followed. Tulu leppuni/leppu/lāvu may involve local aphaeresis/contraction or another root; DEN1 corrects lāvu for earlier levu. Badaga aḷu/avu/au exemplifies lateral lenition/loss. Gondi R Epic aḍusānā could reflect contact and is not needed to establish native retention.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 282; DEN1 1972 p.400 entry 240; PSS83 pp.14–15; K03 p.193

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṛ̆untu/aṛ̆uttu and Malayalam aṛ̆untuka/aṛ̆uttuka independently support high u and transitivity-related dental extensions. Kannada aṛ̆du beside addu preserves an intermediate medial cluster.

Direction. Southern high-vowel stems and retained Kannada ẓd provide a direct route to Telugu dd by medial syncope and assimilation. No language in the reviewed set requires initial apical movement.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aẓ-unt/utt > *aẓd > addu in Telugu/Kannada; Kannada ajju and Kota aj require an additional local palatal-cluster development. Tulu arduni retains a rhotic-plus-stop cluster. The details of dental voicing/strengthening are conditional, but initial-vowel deletion is unnecessary.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. DEDR’s possible link to long-root d396 āẓ could change the remote root quantity; retain that as a sensitivity issue rather than assign long input from an uncertain cross-reference. Gadaba addap blot closely resembles Telugu addu and could be a loan; donor evidence is not explicit, so do not count it as independent phonological confirmation.

Mechanism scope. Medial syncope and cluster assimilation; independent palatal outcomes

Scholarly references. DEDR 285 and tentative cross-reference 396

Independent input evidence. Tamil aḷ strength and Kannada aḷa/aḷavu/aḷavi support short a and postvocalic lateral independently. Telugu alavi/alavu retain exactly the kind of low-vowel expansion compared in measure d295.

Direction. Independent southern vowel-first forms and Konda alvi favor *aḷav > lāv. The long Konda āl is a retained-order quantity variant, not evidence of an original initial lā-.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Treat d291 and d295 as one conservative root family: Kannada/Telugu repeat alavi/alavu and lāvu with overlapping size, power and capacity meanings. This does not assert that every measurement-verb suffix was already part of one undifferentiated proto-lexeme. DEDR’s comparison with long-root d399 is tentative and should be tested as a quantity alternative. Konda lāvu much resembles the Telugu broad adjective and may be borrowed.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aḷa/aḷavu/aḷappu, Kannada aḷe/aḷavu and Kodagu aḷa independently support low a and postvocalic lateral. Telugu alavi supplies a retained related measure noun.

Direction. SD I and retained Telugu alavi support earlier *aḷav rather than initial *lāv with repeated prothesis. Kui/Kuvi/Pengo initial apical forms are therefore innovations under the shared measurement comparison.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aḷ-av > *ḷāv > lāvu in Telugu, with separate ḷ>l. Related palatal extensions give Kuvi/Pengo lāc and Kui ḍās/ḍāc, requiring local lateral-to-stop correspondence. Tulu aḷapuni > lappuni is compatible with aphaeresis and strengthening; K03 p.117 explicitly groups its short-vowel counterpart under aphaeresis.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu alavi and lāvu are not independent roots. Tulu short lapp- should not be equated uncritically with Telugu long lāv-. Manda lēc has unexplained e, so quantity/quality tests exclude it pending a supported vowel history. Badaga ādu measured has an explicitly cited archaic aldu precursor, evidence for lateral loss plus contraction/lengthening, not promotion. Toda’s Q in the DEDR digital tense string is a transcription issue; retain raw data and use independent Toda citation for order.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil aḷai/aḷa/aḷavu and Malayalam aḷayuka independently support low a and lateral after the vowel. Kannada aḷa/aḷavu agree; Telugu alamu has a different labial extension from lāyu.

Direction. The southern comparison and retained Telugu alamu favor V–ḷ. Initial l in Telugu lāyu and Konda/Pengo lap is innovative, but their different final formations prevent a single inferred vowel-quantity derivation.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aḷ-ay > *ḷāy > Telugu lāyu, with lateral merger; *aḷ-am > alamu retains order. Konda/Pengo *aḷ-p > lap/lab is one possible consonantal-formation displacement route; deriving them by shortening earlier *lāp requires independent evidence. Brahui halling retains a before l after initial h addition; h is not evidence for loss of the root vowel.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Mix/measure d295 share similar shapes but are not merged just because their roots are homophonous. Brahui ha in and hatining are associated morphological comparisons in the source; they are not independently counted as three reflexes of this root. Exact origin of Brahui h and stem grades requires its local grammar. Konda/Pengo short vowels may test formative conditioning once their earlier suffix is recovered.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 296; Brahui comparison cites Emeneau 1962 p.63

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Exclude this from the decisive word-initial sound-law denominator unless the free base or date of composition can be established in Telugu. Independent input evidence. Tamil aḷi and Malayalam aḷi/aḷikkuka independently establish high i; Kannada aḷipu/aḷupu supports related high-vowel labial formations. Telugu lā̃cu has a distinct nasal-palatal extension.

Direction. Agreement of Tamil, Malayalam and Kannada favors earlier aḷi-. Telugu initial l is plausibly displaced, but neither its long ā nor the nasal-palatal suffix may be used to invent a low formative in the input.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *aḷ-i-NC > *ḷaNC > lā̃cu would require later nasal loss with compensatory lengthening or a different independently reconstructed extension. A direct a+i > ā contraction conflicts with the short-vowel branch of K03 Rule 20. Without a matching derivative, the exact quantity history is unresolved.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This is a candidate counterexample to an unrestricted prediction of short output after high-i input, not grounds for quietly changing i to a. Kota ayḷ mog twin children is semantically indirect; its glide/lateral order and relationship to unlinked ayḷ classificatory brother-in-law (f_cynufhnk3o6sm) need separate checking. The DEDR parse ayḷ with gloss mog twin children truncates the expression; Wolf’s source preserves the whole expression.

Independent input evidence. Tamil aḷukku, Malayalam aḷukkuka, Kannada aḷuku and Telugu aluku independently establish high u following a singleton lateral. The database *nari jackal head and reconstruction record are unrelated contamination, excluded from historical inference.

Direction. Vowel-before-lateral order agrees across the southern languages and Telugu. Tulu aḷkuni shows medial syncope without initial promotion.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aḷ-uk(k) > Tamil aḷukku, Kannada aḷuku, Telugu aluku; *aḷ-uk > Tulu aḷk-/alk-. Kannada -ar and -ik extensions and local l/ḷ variation are separate developments.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Fear d306 and anger/pricking d304 overlap in Kannada aḷaku/aḷuku and Telugu aluku with related affective semantics; conservative sensitivity should collapse them. Retention cannot be explained by a root geminate: the geminate is the later velar, while the target lateral is singleton. Telugu aḷuku = aluku is an editorial equivalence string, not a third lexical root.

Independent input evidence. Kannada aḷur and Telugu alamu independently agree on initial aḷ/al but have different high versus low medial vowels and final formatives. Konda almi supplies vowel-first lateral plus labial consonant.

Direction. Vowel-first ordering in Kannada and Konda supports the retained Telugu alamu as an earlier-type stem; Telugu lā̃ncu/lā̃pu are innovated formations under the cognacy.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *aḷ-a-NC > *ḷāNC > lā̃ncu, with nasal developments, and related noun lā̃pu. Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The source gives lā̃ncu as intransitive and lā̃pu as its noun; the latter was absent from the parsed group and is explicitly supplemented from DEDR p.29. Kannada aḷur does not independently prove the low vowel required by a simple long-output derivation. Compare mix/seize d296 alamu as a family-overlap sensitivity; the evidence does not warrant silently merging desire d301 merely because its lā̃cu looks similar.

Independent input evidence. Tamil aḷai, Malayalam aḷa and Kota aḷ independently support vowel-first *aḷay. Malayalam aḷḷāppu and Kurux alap add labial morphology; Telugu lā̃ga has a different velar/nasal extension. The displayed **aḷVppV head must not erase this mismatch.

Direction. The southern vowel-first base supports innovative initial l in Telugu, but the exact velar formation is not recovered solely from Telugu. Kurux lātā has different final morphology from alap and cannot automatically be called the same metathesis.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *aḷ-aŋk > *ḷāŋk > Telugu lā̃ga requires an unattested but morphologically plausible velar extension; *aḷay plus a later noun suffix is an alternative. Kurux alap > lātā cannot follow by initial a loss alone because p/t differs. Badaga ae can follow lateral loss in *aḷay without initial promotion.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. PSS83 p.56 example63 proposes moving Toda oḷb to the concealment family (old DED853, current d1015), because a before ay should not yield Toda o. That objection depends on comparing the identical ay formation; an independently justified different labial derivative could weaken it. Keep Toda cognacy ambiguous. The Kurub. aḷe source is mislabeled Malayalam and its precise lect is unresolved; neither it nor the parsed heading is counted as Malayalam evidence.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṟaŋ-kai, Telugu aṟa-cēyi/aṟa-kālu and Kolami ārankei/árungkei independently attest an aṟ/an-bearing first component in body-part compounds. Its precise sense and nasal segmentation are unresolved.

Direction. All source forms retain a vowel before the apical. These are initial compound members, so the compound boundary is after the candidate sequence rather than before it as in saltpan d299.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṟa(n)+kai gives the compared palm compounds, with hand replaced by Telugu cēyi and foot kālu in parallel formations. Kolami length and n/ŋ variants have separate source histories; no initial apical displacement occurs.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The source explicitly says ārankei has n, not ŋ. The parser split that editorial correction into fragments, including a spurious standalone ŋ. Do not count the compound as a bare free root; equally, a following compound boundary alone cannot explain its retention, since anvil d86 changes in that position. Possible connection to half/inner/partition vocabulary needs independent semantic evidence.

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṟi, Malayalam aṟiyuka, Kannada aṟi and the independent K03 *aṯ-V reconstruction support a vowel-first alveolar root. Telugu eṟũgu has a distinct high-u velar/nasal extension; rare Tamil aruku supports investigating that formation but has a different rhotic spelling.

Direction. Agreement of multiple southern languages and Brahui vowel-before-r favors V–alveolar order. Telugu eṟũgu is therefore a retained candidate, not a metathesized item concealed merely by initial e.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṯ-V > southern aṟi; regional *a/eṟ-uk/ŋk > Telugu eṟũgu/eṟuka retains initial order while vowel and formative changes occur. Kota *ar-y > ayr is a separate glide/apical transposition; Brahui harrifing has initial h while preserving vowel-before-r.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. PSS83 p.229 explicitly lists the Telugu know form among exceptions to generalized apical metathesis. Unknown age and vowel of its exact extended input limit a fully specified law test, but are not proof that it was ineligible. Kolami erka is explicitly a Telugu loan. Badaga aḷi search has an unexplained lateral beside ari/aru forms and is not normalized to r.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 314; PSS83 p.229; K03 reconstruction; Hockings & Pilot-Raichoor 1992 pp.28–29,38

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṟu, Malayalam aṟuka and Kannada aṟu independently establish a high-u sever root; Tamil aṟal supplies a separate low-vowel detachment formation. Telugu aṟu retains the root, while ṟakku/rakku has a velar extension.

Direction. Broad southern vowel-first evidence and Brahui harring support earlier V–alveolar ordering. Telugu scratch ṟakku is innovative under this cognacy; the velar derivative’s exact vowel is not automatically identical to that of the bare sever stem.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṯ-u > Telugu aṟu; conditional *aṟ-uk(k) > *ṟakk > ṟakku/rakku gives short a after a different high vowel. Alternative consonantal *aṟ-kk formation yields the same output, so suffix-vowel identity is not uniquely recovered. Brahui harring adds h before the retained vowel-r sequence.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. K61 p.56’s proposed comparison for Telugu rālu invokes Tamil aṟal from this family, linking it to d233 as an alternative analysis. Do not count this source cross-family borrowing of evidence twice. Kolami/Naikri ark may instead belong to cut d175. DEDR also compares n-initial naṟukku d3625: initial n loss versus separate lexical roots needs testing. Badaga place/plant compounds and archaic harakada do not all have equally secure cognacy.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 315 p.29; K61 p.56; cross-references d175,233,3625

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṟu digest and Kannada aragu/aṟave independently support vowel-first apical and different extensions. Telugu aṟugu, Konda aṟgi and Kuvi arg provide a directly comparable regional velar stem.

Direction. SD I and SD II agree on vowel-before-apical in the core digestion comparison. Tulu reñjuni and Gondi rokk are initial-r outliers whose vowels and extensions must be checked before accepting metathesis.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṟ-Vk > Telugu aṟugu, Konda aṟgi and Kuvi arg with regional vowel/syncope differences. Tulu arkame/akku supplies a plausible medial rk>kk route. Conditional *ar-Vñc > reñjuni would require initial loss/displacement plus a separately supported e history.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Original DEDR explicitly questions the Gondi rokkānā/rokk comparison; its o and kk cannot be explained by writing an invented earlier *oru solely to fit it. Kui ārgagāṭi giva is a full light-verb construction whose nominal component may have a contact history. The indigestion subentry has ṟ/ẓ variation and different nouns; do not treat every nasal/velar form as the same input.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 316(a,b) p.30, original question mark on Gondi checked

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṟu and aṟuppu fort independently support the high-u base and labial formation; Telugu aṟupu is a keep/preserve verb. Tamil aṟai camp has a different low-vowel formation.

Direction. Both languages preserve a before the alveolar, supporting the compared regional input. No displaced form is attested in this group.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṟ-u-p > Telugu aṟupu; Tamil stronger *aṟ-u-pp > aṟuppu fort. Tamil aṟku/alku may reflect medial syncope and consonant variation but are explicitly questioned by the source.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. A two-language semantic bridge between dwell and preserve is plausible, not certain. A independently established early Telugu p-formation would strengthen its status as a counterexample to general metathesis; no such date is inferred just from modern retention. Do not explain it away as a free root: the Telugu form is visibly extended.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṟai and Kannada aṟacu/aṟicu/aṟucu independently establish V–alveolar ordering and several extensions; Telugu aṟacu/aṟapu supply retained related forms. The exact input of rajju is less specific than the head *aṟ-a.

Direction. Multiple southern vowel-first forms favor earlier aṟ-. Telugu initial ṟ/r formations are innovative under the cognacy. Naiki arap and Gadaba arg support retained initial order outside SD I/Telugu.

Derivation and relative chronology. K61 p.55 compares rajju with consonantal *ar-j; Telugu ṟaŋke can reflect a nasal-velar derivative with displacement, while aṟacu/aṟapu retain order. Kui ṛaspa has a separate s/p cluster; its origin is not explained by simply adding -pa to modern Telugu. Kannada racce may reflect local displacement plus strengthening, but its cognacy/contact history remains unresolved.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Kannada racce was stranded in a gloss and would be missed by a search limited to Form; it is source-verified and added as one research observation. Gondi rāŋ(g) is explicitly queried by DEDR, so its long vowel does not automatically confirm a shared innovation. Kolami raz could be inherited or borrowed; no automatic Telugu loan is assumed. Koraga ajike lacks r and needs a local cluster-loss/cognacy explanation.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 319 p.30, original entry checked; K61 p.55 §1.130

PropertyAnnotation

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṟai, Kannada aṟe and Kota ar independently support a vowel-first alveolar and an ay formation; Toda aṟ corroborates the consonant class. Telugu ṟāyi/rāyi preserves two rhotic spellings.

Direction. The shared SD I vowel-first forms favor *aṯ/ṟ-ay > ṟāy, not widespread insertion before an original *ṟāy. Kannada rāyi is explicitly borrowed from Telugu and cannot support an inherited Kannada innovation.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṟ-ay > *ṟāy > Telugu ṟāyi > rāyi, with later ṟ/r merger. Short ṟappa small stone has a different strong labial extension; *aṟ-pp > ṟapp is plausible, but shortening an earlier long vowel is not uniquely supported.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Badaga are is the lexical evidence; dozens of place names containing it are dependent derivatives and count as one family, with historical labels preserved. The precise *ṯ versus *ṟ reconstruction depends on the wider alveolar correspondence; modern Kannada is not assumed to preserve the proto manner of articulation.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 321; DEN1 1972 p.400 entry 271; Hockings & Pilot-Raichoor 1992 p.30

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṟai and Malayalam aṟa independently support singleton alveolar and ay formation; Telugu aṟa beside aṟṟa shows strengthening in a regional variant. Tulu adɛ has a stop reflex.

Direction. Shared vowel-first ordering supports older aṟay. Telugu singleton aṟa cannot be excluded from an eligible input class merely because the same entry also has a strengthened variant.

Derivation and relative chronology. *aṟay > Tamil aṟai, Malayalam aṟa, Telugu aṟa; regional gemination yields Telugu aṟṟa and potentially Gondi arra. Tulu adɛ and Badaga -ādu require local alveolar/stop and quantity histories, without initial relocation.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This is a near input match to displaced rock d321: a short initial vowel, singleton alveolar and ay noun. Different meanings do not create a phonological condition. Gondi arrā/arra could reflect Telugu contact; Muria ahpi has a substantially different cluster requiring an independent account. Badaga attests only compound components, so their word-boundary eligibility differs.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 322 p.30; compare DEDR 321
