Independent input evidence. Kannada anu/anavu/anuvu, Telugu anuvu and Kota anv support a nasal after the initial vowel and a labial extension. Tamil a/aṁ beauty is explicitly questioned; DEDR compares c-initial cannu d2423.

Direction. The regional vowel-first nasal input is supported independently of Telugu. A possible earlier initial c loss does not imply n has subsequently exchanged with a.

Derivation and relative chronology. *an-V-v > Telugu anuvu and Kannada anavu/anuvu, Kota anv by medial syncope; Tulu anutana adds another nominal formative. No initial nasal displacement is observed.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Use as a nasal control, not as an automatic test of a rule restricted to nonnasal apicals. The Tamil loss/nasalization comparison and possible older c-bearing root need separate reconstruction. Vowel quality of the intervening syllable is variable rather than fixed from Telugu alone.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 328 p.30 and cross-reference 2423

Eligibility / caveatnasal-control

Independent input evidence. Tamil aṉuppu and Malayalam anuppuka independently establish high u and nasal before labial; Telugu anupu preserves the uncontracted order. Kannada ampaka, Kurux ambnā and Malto ambe support a consonantal nasal-labial variant.

Direction. Independent uncontracted southern forms plus Telugu anupu show that ampu need not reflect initial nasal metathesis: medial vowel deletion and place assimilation are sufficient.

Derivation and relative chronology. *an-up > *anp > amp gives Telugu ampu and related labial-cluster forms; Telugu anucu/ancu needs a separate palatal extension or stem remodeling, not a p-to-c change assumed without context. Brahui hamp- adds initial h while preserving a before the nasal cluster.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. These are related derivatives and must count once per root. The relationship between full-vowel and consonantal formations could partly be inherited morphology rather than one universal syncope event. Gadaba anisp load on cart has an i/s extension whose history is not supplied by the basic send comparison.

Mechanism scope. Medial vowel loss and nasal place assimilation, no initial nasal displacement

Scholarly references. DEDR 329; Kobayashi 2022 reconstruction record *anVp-; Brahui source cites Emeneau 1962 p.63

d410 — proximal demonstratives and adverbs

d410: proximal demonstratives and adverbs

PropertyAnnotation
Primary familydeictic-a-i
Comparative input*i-t(u), *i-w-an/-ar; oblique *id-an-i / *iw-an-i, *iw-att-i
Initial consonantØ
V1 quality / quantityi / short deictic input; secondary long formations
C2 identity / structuret/w/b / morphological dental/labial elements
Following vowela/i/u/variable
Root/formation shapedeictic base + gender/number + oblique augment
Grammatical categorypronoun/adverb
Boundary evidenceGender/number and oblique augments; proximal and distal members of one productive paradigm.
Input classpronominal-morphology
Telugu hypothesisoutside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule
Input confidencehigh for order; medium for immediate oblique prehistory
Overall confidencemedium
Eligibility / caveatmorphological-pronoun-domain

Independent input evidence. Tamil itu/ivaṉ, Malayalam itu/ivaṇ, Kannada idu/iva and Pengo/Manda idi/ivan establish initial i followed by gender/number material. The a- oblique augment is independently comparative in the matching distal paradigm (K03 p.222); the lexical source does not independently supply every uncontracted proximal oblique.

Direction. The a:i demonstrative opposition and the same following morphology across several branches support vowel-before-dental/labial input. Konda deni is particularly valuable because it does not simply copy the surface Telugu high vowel in dīni.

Derivation and relative chronology. K03 proposes lowering in *id-an-i > *ed-an-i before displacement/contraction, followed by Konda deni, while Telugu dīni is remodeled to preserve the opposition to interrogative dēni; this is analogy, not a phonetic i+a>ī rule. Compare *iw-an-i > Konda veni versus Telugu vīni, modern plural vīṭi from *iw-att-i with corresponding analogical possibilities. Konda ibe/ibeṇi : bēn/bēṇi supplies labial locative restructuring; Pengo ibe/ibṇi retains initial i even with syncope.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The anti-homophony account for Telugu dīni is a plausible hypothesis (K03 p.223 n.14), not demonstrated by a directly attested earlier *deni stage. Sastri1969 pp.178,184 explicitly treats historical dēni as interrogative; an inscriptional English translation this grant is not sufficient to identify a proximal ancestral stage. Konda current DB plural oblique venka differs from K03 veni: preserve both source claims and do not silently replace morphology. Konda short deni versus long bēn shows formation-specific quantity. This cannot be used to validate a single phonetic outcome rule for all pronouns. Te nisuvu/nisũgu child is a separate semantic/cognacy issue within the giant deictic entry and is not evidence for nasal metathesis of the deictic base. Direct and oblique forms are research-split with links to their original unsplit database records.

Mechanism scope. Morphologically restricted displacement/contraction; Telugu high vowels plausibly analogical, not independent evidence for phonetic output.

Scholarly references. DEDR410; Krishnamurti2003 pp.158,222–223 nn.13–14

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭi/iṭa, Malayalam iṭika/iṭakka, Kannada iḍi/iḍupu and Telugu iḍiyu/iḍupu support vowel-first order and more than one formative vowel independently.

Direction. Agreement on initial i before the apical across several branches favors earlier iṭ-, without assuming the Tamil forms alone are conservative.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭ-i > Telugu iḍiyu, Kannada iḍi; *iṭ-u-p > iḍupu in both. Kota/Toda lose final/medial vowels but retain the initial vowel. Irula ḍepisu may involve local aphaeresis after vowel lowering, but the source does not supply its immediate earlier form.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Irula is an uncertain local initial-loss candidate, not evidence that the Telugu innovation was shared with Irula. The nasal in iṇḍe needs a separate formation history. Pengo d2955 and Kolami d2974 are explicitly tentative comparisons and are not silently added to this root. Badaga idi is source-marked uncertain; do not treat hamlet Idukore as another root.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 432; cross-references 2955,2974 remain tentative

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭam/iṭai, Malayalam iṭam/eṭam and Kannada iḍe/eḍe agree on vowel-first i/e plus apical; Kota eṛm preserves the nominal m.

Direction. The shared vowel-first forms establish the pre-displacement order. Southern i/e alternation supports lowering before a, not a proto-initial d.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭ-am > *eḍam > Telugu eḍamu; *iṭ-ay > *eḍay > eḍa/eḍe. Kota and Toda shorten the word by final loss while keeping the first vowel. Tulu source contains dekki alongside iḍɛ, a likely local initial-loss formation with gemination.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Merge d434 with interval d448 for primary root counts: Tamil iṭai and Telugu eḍa/eḍamu recur with intersecting place/space senses. This avoids counting one spatial noun twice. The exact relationship of Tulu dekki to the other nominal formations remains unresolved and it is not automatically a SCDr-type contraction.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam iṭar, Kannada iḍaru/iḍuru and Old Telugu eḍaṟu support initial vowel plus apical. Tamil iṭumpai and Telugu iḍuma independently support a distinct labial/nasal derivative.

Direction. The historical Telugu retained form and southern comparison establish vowel-first ancestry. Telugu ḍepparamu is related semantically but its exact pp-bearing formation is not independently matched.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭ-ar > *eḍar > eḍaru; *iṭ-um(p) > iḍuma with independent labial changes. A conditional *iṭ-a-ppar > *ḍēppar > ḍeppar with pre-geminate shortening could yield ḍepparamu/depparamu, but the reconstructed extension is not established by iṭar alone.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Treat ḍepparamu as probable displacement with unresolved formation rather than inventing *-appar to guarantee the rule. eḍḍamu/eḍḍami have strengthening or cluster assimilation, not initial metathesis. The older obstruction verb may belong with stumble d437; that family collapse is a sensitivity, not an asserted etymology.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 435; tentative comparison 788

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam iṭaṟ-, Kannada iḍaṟu/eḍaṟu/eḍagu, Tulu eḍaŋkɯ and Malto iṛpe support initial vowel plus retroflex. The velar and rhotic extensions must be distinguished.

Direction. The comparative vowel-first order and Tulu dialect doublets establish earlier V–ṭ; Telugu ḍekku has shifted/lost the initial vowel under this cognacy.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *iṭ-a-k(k) > *eḍakk > *ḍēkk > ḍekku with shortening before kk. Tulu eḍaŋkɯ > ḍaŋkɯ/daŋkɯ is independently described as dialectal aphaeresis (K03 p.116), not a required same event. Kannada Havyaka ḍaŋku and Koraga ḍakki could be local losses or contact forms.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The Telugu vowel e fits lowered *i before a, but its exact kk formation remains uncertain. Tulu dompu/dumpiyuni and doŋkɯ have labial/velar alternatives and rounded vowels that initial loss alone does not explain. Neither matching initial ḍ nor geographic proximity proves shared ancestry. Badaga erandu is source-uncertain and has an unexplained nasal sequence.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 437; DEN1 1972 p.400 entry 371; K03 p.116 citing Kekunnaya 1994 pp.42–44

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭi flour/confection and iṭiyappam, Malayalam iṭiyappam and Telugu iḍi/iḍikuḍumu agree on the vowel-first food base.

Direction. Independent southern food compounds corroborate vowel-first iṭi; there is no evidence here for a proto-initial ḍi.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭi > Telugu iḍi; appam/kuḍumu are separate compound components. The high-i match makes this a formal comparison to beat d443, but food-name diffusion may be later than the native change.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Possible relation to pounding/beat and to iṭṭali d455 must be considered in family sensitivity. Do not count each kind of cake as an independent negative. Culinary borrowing chronology is unresolved, so retain it as a lexical control rather than use it alone to falsify an inherited law.

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭu : iṭṭ-, Kannada iḍu : iṭṭ-, Telugu iḍu, and matching Central Dravidian paradigms independently support high u and vowel-first root. Long īḍu nouns are a separate quantity formation.

Direction. Broad family distribution, including Kui/Kuvi/Pengo/Manda retention, supports original iṭ- order and rules out using Tulu dīpini as the reconstructive starting point.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭ-u > iḍu/ɨḍ-; past *iṭ-ṭ remains geminate in many languages. Gondi intervocalic ṭ corresponds to rhotic in ir/irr, Konda iṟ-, without initial relocation. Tulu dīpini beside iḍpini may show displacement, analogical remodeling or interaction with long īḍɯ; a literal *i+u contraction to ī is not established.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The initial apical is singleton in the nonpast, despite past gemination; do not exclude the whole root as a geminate. Tulu dīḍɯ/jīḍɯ/ījɯ/īḍɯ require a linked paradigm/causative history, potentially d addition or expressive reinforcement; their shared ī is not evidence for a universal metathesis rule. Long nouns and aspectual auxiliary uses are not additional etyma.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 442; K03 Rule20 pp.157–158

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭi, Malayalam iṭi/iṭikka and Kannada iḍi independently support i+i, while Tamil iṭu and Kannada iḍaku support other formations. Kota/Toda, Kolami, Pengo and Kurux have vowel-first root cognates.

Direction. The independent high-i formation supports earlier iṭi > Telugu ḍī. Konda ṛey/ṛī were incorrectly assigned Kolami in the database: source p.43 makes Kolami iṛ- retained and Konda innovated.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭ-i > *ḍii > ḍī is a possible implementation of Rule20a; same-quality high vowels meet its contraction condition. Konda *iṭV > ṛī/ṛey involves its own apical correspondence and vowel variants. Kannada ḍī/ḍīku/ḍikki beside iḍi may be a Telugu loan, expressive reinforcement, or local displacement; no donor date yet decides.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not count Kannada and Telugu identical impact nouns automatically as independent changes. Telugu ḍīkonu is a light-verb/compound extension of ḍī, not another etymon. Imported Badaga sickle/iron-saw records have possible cut/iron segmentation rather than the beat root; their linkage is questionable and not used as a decisive control. The Konda correction reverses which comparison language appears to innovate.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 443 p.43 directly inspected; K03 Rule6 p.107 and Rule20 p.157

d444 — pinch, pincers, tongs

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam iṭukku and iṭukki independently support high u after ṭ. Kannada iḍaku provides a low-vowel variant, while Old Kannada iẓkuẓi has a different apical and internal structure.

Direction. Vowel-first southern pinch verbs favor earlier V–apical order, but the tool nouns do not all share an independently recoverable complete stem.

Derivation and relative chronology. Tamil *iṭ-uk > iṭukku retains order. Kannada ikkuẓ and Tulu ikkuḷ may involve medial assimilation of the first apical, leaving another apical after k; alternatively their internal apical order reflects a different noun formation. Kui ḍīpa is an initial-displacement candidate, but i+u does not straightforwardly produce ī and its labial noun suffix differs.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. No Telugu attestation in this database group: record a gap, not a failure to change. Reconstructing *iṭi-pp solely to predict Kui ī would be circular. A source paradigm connecting the pinch verb to a labial noun, or an independently attested i-bearing formative, would distinguish contraction from another etymology. The superficial k/l reversal in tongs needs its own analysis, not the initial-metathesis label.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 444 p.43 directly checked

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭṭaḷam, Kannada iṭṭaḷa/iṭṭaṇa and Telugu iṭṭalamu independently support a geminate target in this formation, alongside a singleton high-u narrowness family iṭukku/iḍuku.

Direction. Both formations preserve initial i/e across southern languages; singleton and geminate stems must be classified separately before comparing Telugu.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭṭ-aḷ-am > Telugu iṭṭalamu with lateral simplification; crowded mass > abundant is independently bridged by Kannada meanings. The iṭ-uk narrowness words retain a singleton ṭ before a velar formative and cannot be treated as the identical input to iṭṭalamu.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu is a geminate-formation control, not proof that its singleton *iṭuk input resisted metathesis: that input is not attested in Telugu here. Gadaba iḍigeda a few has different morphology and possible contact, while Badaga glade/nook and place names have queried etymologies. Broad connection with spatial d434/d448 or distress d435 is plausible but unproven.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭai, Malayalam iṭayikka and Telugu eḍayu/eḍavu independently support vowel-first ordering with low second vowel; Malto eṛare provides a northern order comparison.

Direction. Retained southern and northern orders favor an earlier vowel-first root. Telugu davvu is likely related to eḍavu, but its a and geminate vv require more than simply exchanging the initial e and ḍ.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭ-ay > *eḍay > eḍayu regularly retains the initial vowel. A displacement analysis of davvu would require an earlier vowel or analogical variant, plus vv strengthening/shortening; *eḍ-av > *ḍēv does not directly yield davvu. Kolami davva/dautān and Naikri dʰāv may be Telugu-area loans, not independent support for the missing steps.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. K03 p.57 explicitly doubts the derivation of davvu/dhāv from *iṭ-a; his alternative discussion concerns voiced aspiration and a possible older laryngeal, not a demonstrated solution. Brahui is explicitly questioned in DEDR p.43. Nahali dhava is a contact-zone comparison, not a Dravidian cognate vote. The spatial-root relation to d434/d448 is a sensitivity hypothesis; do not silently explain the vowel by assuming different proto-roots.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 446 p.43 directly checked, including question mark before Brahui; K03 p.57 explicitly questions the etymology of davvu/dhāv

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭai weary is the sole independent unshifted witness in this entry. Telugu ḍayyu and Kuvi ḍah/daha/ḍāh agree semantically, but the imported initial *ḍaj reconstruction simply repeats the innovated-looking order.

Direction. Tamil vowel-first order, general apical correspondences, and Kuvi y/h comparison favor earlier *iṭay, provisionally; with only one unshifted branch, prothesis or imperfect cognacy cannot be ruled out on majority arithmetic.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *iṭay > an initial ḍay stem gives Telugu ḍayyu and Kuvi ḍah; the expected lowered/contracted ē and actual a are not reconciled. Kuvi length varies by source/lect. Kolami ḍay is explicitly a Telugu loan. Sastri 1969 p.111 derives Telugu dappi thirst from dayyu weary, offering an alternative to d109 aṭ-/aṇṭ- ancestry.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not invent an unattested *aṭay just to match a. The fatigue-to-thirst derivative is semantically and morphologically plausible (compare noccu/noppi in Sastri), but it needs historical attestation and comparison with southern thirst cognates before merging d109. It also must remain separate from homophonous destruction ḍappi d277.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 447 p.44; Sastri 1969 p.111, image verified (PDF136)

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṭai/iṭam, Malayalam iṭam/eṭam, Kannada eḍa and Telugu eḍama support earlier vowel-first i/e plus retroflex. Kota/Toda and Kodagu agree in order, though vowel quality differs.

Direction. Telugu ḍā/dā is innovated relative to the comparative vowel-first left-side noun, but cannot be assigned the expected ē contraction without an additional vowel history. Tulu damma/datta has strengthening and local initial loss.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṭam > *eḍam > eḍama is retained. Aphaeresis/clipping of an already a-bearing derivative, analogy with regional left-side words, or displacement followed by vowel change may underlie ḍā/dā; the current source does not select one. Kolami edamakei is explicitly a Telugu loan and was mislabeled Telugu in the parsed corpus.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. DEDR separately assigns many other SCDr left words to Indo-Aryan *ḍavva/*ḍevva: Kui deba/debe/debo, Kuvi tebri, Gondi ḍema/demar/ḍāvā, etc. Those are a loan comparison, not absent cognates or shared metathesis. Source-only loan observations are inventoried separately. Naiki ḍākiyan kī may reflect regional borrowing; its full donor is unresolved.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 449 p.44; CDIAL 5539 loan comparison; source headings directly checked

Independent input evidence. Kurux iṛnā and Malto eṛye agree on vowel before retroflex rhotic. This two-language comparison does not recover a uniquely Proto-Dravidian ṭ/ẓ input or a formative vowel.

Direction. Both attested branches preserve V–ṛ; there is no displacement contrast from which to infer an earlier opposite order.

Derivation and relative chronology. Regional *i/eṛ- plus distinct Kurux -nā and Malto -ye endings gives the forms with order retained. The first-vowel correspondence needs the wider Kurux–Malto system, not an outcome-selected assumption.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Retain as a northern apical-root comparison, with Telugu and other SCDr unattested. It does not create seven negatives for languages with no cognate. The imported reconstruction is regional even when the interface groups it under PDr.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 451 p.44

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Treat Gondi as a probable but uncertain displacement case, not a dialectal Kolami D/R alternation. More wall nouns or a source derivational base could establish V2 and direction. No Telugu form is supplied; this is a comparative gap there.

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṇai/iṇaŋku, Malayalam iṇa/iṇayuka, Kannada eṇe and Telugu ena/enayu support a retroflex nasal after an initial vowel, and low formative independently.

Direction. Agreement supports earlier iṇ-, with Telugu ṇ>n and southern lowering. Telugu nenayu retains a second n as well as an initial n, so it is not the result of simply moving the sole root nasal.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṇ-ay > *eṇay > enayu; derivative enucu/enupu has distinct palatal/labial morphology. nenayu can reflect added n through rebracketing or analogical reinforcement, but a source context is needed to choose. Tamil eḷḷu equal is explicitly questioned by DEDR and is not secure proof of a nasal/lateral root alternation.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. A control for the published exclusion of nasal C2. The initial n in nenayu cannot be counted as metathesis on surface inspection. The n survives medially, so deletion-plus-insertion or morphology would be required under a movement account. Comparison with iẓai d507 is tentative.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 457 p.44 directly checked; K03 Rule20 excludes nasal apicals

Independent input evidence. Tamil ira/iravu, Malayalam iravu/irakkuka, Kannada era/eravu and Telugu eravu independently support i/e before r and a low formative.

Direction. The widespread vowel-first form, corroborated by Malto irɣre, favors original ir-; Tulu randuni is innovated under this comparison.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ir-av > *erav > Telugu eravu preserves the order despite an input that could permit contraction. Tulu randuni may follow initial vowel loss in a nasal-bearing begging formation; its exact preceding full form is not attested here.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not explain Telugu retention by assigning an unsupported high formative: southern av words directly match its loan noun. Late lexical borrowing remains possible but is not documented, so this stays a genuine low-vowel retention counterexample. Tulu verbal morphology differs from eravu and does not prove a shared event.

PropertyAnnotation

Input classmixed-or-uncertain-quantity
Telugu hypothesisoutside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule
Input confidencehigh
Overall confidencehigh
Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iru-/īr, Kannada iru/ir and eraḍu, Central Dravidian ir- forms and Brahui irā/iraṭ support vowel-first order independently. Nonhuman aṇṭ and human u-var formations can be distinguished by their morphology before their outcomes are inspected.

Direction. Wide independent retention of bound ir-/īr and the different human and nonhuman derivatives favors earlier ir-, not original r- with prothesis throughout the family. The shared r-initial nonhuman numeral across SCDr is strong comparative evidence, but recent Tamil/Malayalam/Tulu initial loss must be evaluated separately.

Derivation and relative chronology. K03 pp.159–160: *ir-aṇṭ > *eraṇḍ > hypothetical *rēṇḍ > Telugu reṇḍu with shortening before a nasal-stop cluster; other SCDr *ir-i/u-ṇṭ > *rīṇḍ with variable shortening and Konda backing to runḍi. Human *iru-var remains vowel-first in Telugu iruvuru and Gondi irvur; r+v assimilation yields Kannada/Old Telugu ibbar forms. Tamil/Malayalam/Tulu aphaeresis produces reṇṭu/raṇṭu/raḍḍɯ in later language histories. Malto *irw > iwr (corpus ivr) is a separate medial consonant transposition.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not count human, nonhuman, twenty, two hundred and ordinal derivatives as independent roots. Telugu retained iru/īr is a bound root and cannot be treated as an identical free-word input to reṇḍu. The short Telugu output does not prove that a long intermediate existed; *rēṇḍ is K03’s conditional reconstruction. Kui rīnḍe shows that pre-cluster shortening was not universal across languages. Konda iddum retains an initial vowel in a measure compound and needs separate cluster-assimilation/contact analysis. Kodagu daṇḍɨ, Markodi dad and Badaga ratte require local phonological/contact histories; do not automatically equate them with the SCDr innovation. Kurux ēṇḍ has a vowel history K03 explicitly calls puzzling. Toda ačok/acok is a measure term within an example, not another reflex of two.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 474 p.46 directly checked; K03 pp.159–160 and p.116; Hockings–Pilot-Raichoor 1992 pp.54,86,507; Canvin 2025 lect data

d475 — jujube

d475: jujube

PropertyAnnotation
Primary familyd475
Comparative inputregional *ir-a-; nasal/velar and dental tree-name formations
Initial consonantØ
V1 quality / quantityi / short
C2 identity / structurer/l / singleton
Following vowela
Root/formation shapeVC-a-NC / VC-a-C
Grammatical categorynoun
Boundary evidenceLow vowel independently observed; exact dental/nasal/velar tree-name formatives are not assumed identical.
Input classshort-vowel-initial-singleton-apical
Telugu hypothesiseligible; obligatory application predicts D
Input confidencemedium
Overall confidencemedium
Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil irati/irantai/ilantai, Malayalam ilanta and Kannada era/elaci support an initial vowel and medial liquid independently. The exact nasal-velar formation of Telugu rē̃gu is not matched by every southern tree name.

Direction. Independent retained southern forms favor earlier ir-/il- order. Original DEDR p.46 supplies actual Telugu rē̃gu/rēnu; the database instead mislabeled Kolami rēŋga as Telugu and omitted those Telugu forms.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *ir-aŋk > *eraŋk > *rēŋk > Telugu rē̃gu, with voicing/nasal developments; rēnu requires a different consonant change or variant. Tamil r/l alternation and dental rather than velar suffix need separate formation histories. Malayalam ilanta > lanta is straightforward initial vowel loss.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Kannada rēgu is explicitly borrowed from Telugu. Gondi, Kolami, Naikri/Naiki, Parji and Gadaba rēŋg-type tree names might spread with the plant name; no independent innovation is inferred just from initial r. More southern velar derivatives or historical recipient attestations would discriminate inheritance from diffusion. Malto ilkru has a different cluster. Source supplements do not add roots.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 475 p.46 directly checked; Southworth 2006 imported *irak is a proposal, not an attestation

d476 — deer, antelope

d476: deer, antelope

PropertyAnnotation
Primary familyd476
Comparative input*ir-al-ay, r/l order variation
Initial consonantØ
V1 quality / quantityi / short
C2 identity / structurer / singleton
Following vowela
Root/formation shapeVC-a-C-ay
Grammatical categorynoun
Boundary evidenceWhole deer noun compared; later l/ḍ material in Telugu has no demonstrated identical formative ancestry.
Input classshort-vowel-initial-singleton-apical
Telugu hypothesiseligible; obligatory application predicts D
Input confidencemedium
Overall confidencemedium
Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iralai and Kannada/Tulu eraḷe agree on initial vowel and r before later lateral; Malto ilaru has the liquids in the opposite order. Old Telugu iri also begins with a vowel.

Direction. The southern r...l agreement favors earlier *iral provisionally; Malto may show internal liquid reversal. Telugu lēḍi would require movement of a different liquid and an additional final consonant history, not just initial i/r metathesis.

Derivation and relative chronology. Retained *iralay > eraḷe in Kannada/Tulu; reduced Old Telugu iri and strengthened iṟṟi require morphological/cluster changes. A proposed *ilara > *lēra > lēḍi path would need both an independent liquid reversal and a regular r/ḍ development; neither is established by this set.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. DEDR explicitly prefixes a question mark to Telugu lēṭi/lēḍi. Keep them uncertain rather than forcing them into a lateral-metathesis class. Malto internal reversal is separately plausible but not proved directionally by simple majority. Badaga iya may reflect liquid loss but is source-uncertain. Historical iri is the reliable Telugu retained comparison.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 476 p.46 directly checked, including question mark before lēṭi/lēḍi

Independent input evidence. Tamil iraḷi/iṟali preserves an initial vowel plus two differently ordered-quality liquids. Kannada/Telugu rēla and Gondi rēlā share an r-initial plant name; only Tamil supplies the unshifted word here.

Direction. Earlier *iral- is plausible by the low-vowel contraction correspondence, but a Tamil prothetic adaptation of a regional rēl word remains possible without wider retained evidence.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *iral > *eral > *rēl > Telugu rēla-ceṭṭu; historical ṛēla gives an older r-initial attestation. Gondi rērkā requires an added velar and lateral/rhotic change; Kannada and Gondi may have borrowed the tree name.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not treat the imported *rēl as proved proto-input or Tamil as necessarily conservative. The old Telugu rhotic is transcribed ṛ in this source and should not be assigned a phonetic value without its inscriptional edition. Cassia is a Latin gloss incorrectly parsed as Telugu. Exact cognacy/donor history keeps this out of the decisive reconstructed-input cohort.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil iru/iruppu, Kannada iru/irdu and Kodagu ir- independently support a vowel-first existential root. Telugu iruvu/iravu retains noun formations; Malayalam irippu differs in formative vowel from Tamil iruppu.

Direction. The broad existential comparison favors earlier ir-. Kui rīnda/rīspa is innovative under its related steady/stand meaning, but its high-i length and added consonants require separate reconstruction.

Derivation and relative chronology. Retained *iru-v > Telugu iruvu, with a-bearing iravu; Kannada irke > ikke and Telugu ikka are compatible with medial syncope plus assimilation. Tulu ippuni/itt- can continue r+labial/dental cluster assimilation. Kui *ir-i-nt/*ir-i-sp could yield rīnda/rīspa, but i in those exact formations is not independently established. Kota ig-/ir-/it- is a paradigm, not initial promotion.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Low-vowel Telugu iravu must not be erased by choosing only the high-u root label. Telugu iŋkuva has DEDR’s explicit alternative demonstrative iṅku d420. Kui rītka includes plural morphology and possible consonant-order changes, not another etymon. Badaga negative illa/ille is cross-linked but belongs to a separate negative-base analysis, not straightforward irregular sound change of iru.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 480; DEN1 p.400 entry407; K03 existential reconstruction; alternative d420 for iŋkuva

Independent input evidence. Tamil iru great and irumai greatness provide the independent rhotic comparison; Telugu has inu- in compounds, especially inumikkili very great.

Direction. Tamil rhotic versus Telugu nasal can reflect assimilation before a following m in the compound. There is no evidence of r moving before the initial vowel.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *iru-mikkili > *inu-mikkili by anticipatory nasal influence, followed by extraction/generalization of inu- as a combining form. Compare Telugu inu māṟu twice (d474) and inumu iron (d486), without assuming all three have identical history.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Only a narrow two-language adjective comparison; no free Telugu inu paradigm is supplied, and the corpus inu is an in-construction fragment. Do not classify it as metathesis concealed by r loss unless an initial r-stage is independently attested. Compound-bound status is visible before outcome classification.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Keep the complex plant-name family uncertain for inherited-law counts. The fact that blackwood can be named after darkness is a semantic hypothesis, not evidence for every segment. Tulu kari-bīṭi independently adds black, which can support either reinforcement or a different lexical base. No unsupported chain is selected.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Preserve a high-u control but flag the technical lexeme’s undated dissemination. Independent input evidence. Tamil iruppai/iluppai/irumpai, Malayalam iruppa/iluppa, Tulu irippe and Gondi/Parji irup support initial vowel plus liquid and a labial formation. Kui irpi : ripi directly attests the relevant short closed-syllable alternation.

Direction. Shared vowel-first forms and attested irp clusters favor earlier irup > irp. Kui ripi is an initial i/r reversal of a structure independently present as irpi, unlike Telugu ippa, where the first vowel remains.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ir-up(p) > *irp(p) > Telugu ippa through medial assimilation/loss, matched by Tamil ippai and Kannada ippe. Kui irpi > ripi exchanges initial vowel and rhotic with no added length; this can follow medial syncope. Kuvi irpi retains that same cluster. Gondi hirp/hiruk and long forms have h/quantity/plural morphology separate from initial displacement.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The same plant family offers competing outcomes: retention, medial assimilation and short displacement. It does not establish that metathesis occurred to prevent assimilation as a purposeful process. Konda ipa maran could be an assimilated inherited base or contact form. Badaga irippe kāi is glossed as chironji, not mahua, so cognacy/species association is uncertain and should be checked against d2628.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam irumpu and Kodagu irɨmbɨ support initial vowel, liquid and labial nasal-stop. The proposed initial c belongs to a deeper darkness comparison d2552, not an attested initial consonant in these iron words.

Direction. The independent southern words establish earlier irump- for the regional comparison. Kui rumba has lost the first vowel under a straightforward account; its surviving vowel is the original u, so literal i/r exchange is not independently demonstrated.

Derivation and relative chronology. *irump > Telugu inumu may combine weakening of mp and anticipatory nasal influence on r; the exact sequence is unresolved. Kota/Toda ib requires medial cluster simplification. Kui irumba > rumba is compatible with aphaeresis; a displacement-plus-vowel-assimilation route is possible but adds unsupported steps here.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Iron is a cultural term, so the time of lexical diffusion and possible deep *c loss matter. Neither Telugu n nor absence of r in Kota/Toda proves concealed metathesis. Kolami inum may be borrowed from Telugu; no independent event is counted. Compare inu-mikkili d481 and inu māṟu d474 for a testable r/n-before-m pattern, without declaring it exceptionless yet.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 486; K03 deeper *cir-umpu reconstruction; darkness d2552

Independent input evidence. Tamil irai/iraŋku/irumu and Malayalam irampuka/irumal have vowel-first forms, whereas Kannada/Kodagu/Tulu/Telugu ramp/ramb forms cluster in expressive noise senses. DEDR calls Telugu ṟ probably expressive.

Direction. An earlier iramp with local initial loss is plausible, but expressive r-initial formation and later southern prothesis or contamination also fit. Neither a modern Tamil word nor the imported *ramp head alone establishes direction.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional iramp > ramp by aphaeresis retains the following a. A regular lowered i+a contraction would instead need an explained route from ē to a/shortness; that route is not established. Cough irum- may be a distinct derivative or related expressive formation, not the exact same input as rampu.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Keep this outside the secure inherited input cohort. Sanskrit-like aspirated rambʰa/rambʰāṭa forms warrant a contact/source check; aspiration is not proof of inherited Proto-Dravidian phonology. Parji ran ban is an echo-like expression with a different second component. Need historical unshifted ramp-family attestations or a reliable donor history to choose among analyses.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam il, Konda ilu, Pengo/Manda il and Telugu illu support a monosyllabic lateral root with strengthened free forms. Seven imported *iẓi descend paradigm reconstructions are erroneous links, not alternative house inputs.

Direction. The wide vowel-first house root supports original il. Kui iḍu changes the medial lateral realization without moving it before the initial vowel.

Derivation and relative chronology. *il > illu/illam in free/extended forms; language-specific oblique stems include Telugu iṇṭi and Pengo inj-. Those require oblique suffix/cluster assimilation, not an initial metathesis. Konda ilku and Kuvi ilka preserve a lateral before plural material.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Classify the independently supported VC root and strengthened free form separately from a hypothetical singleton VCV input. Do not use the spurious *iẓi data to predict displacement in house. Kolami iltam is explicitly a Telugu loan tied to residence with a wife’s family; related iltāmā may be contact-associated, whereas ella house is a separate retained-order witness.

Independent input evidence. Tamil ila/ilavam/ilavu, Malayalam ilavu and Kannada elava establish initial vowel and medial lateral independently. Parji neluk has an additional initial nasal; the displayed optional *ń is a hypothesis rather than observed proto-evidence.

Direction. The independent southern il/el forms favor an earlier vowel-first plant name. Eastern lēk is plausibly displaced, but its velar rather than labial ending needs a separate formation history.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *il-a-k > *ela-k > *lēk gives Gondi/Konda/Kuvi lēk. Kuvi ḍākāngi would additionally require l > ḍ and a different formative or plant-name compound; its ā may preserve an earlier suffix vowel only under the cognacy analysis.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. K80 item 3 has no Kui attestation. Kuvi e versus ā is a real dialect/source contrast, not two independent roots. Parji n cannot simply be deleted from reconstruction to obtain a positive case; contact, nasal accretion and an older nasal input remain competing explanations. Badaga muccukikku means veil and is not a relevant tree-name witness.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Boundary evidenceIndependent comparative tense/voice alternations motivate -k/-p, -nt/-ntt formations; not classes invented from outcomes.
Input classshort-vowel-initial-singleton-apical
Telugu hypothesiseligible; obligatory application predicts D
Input confidencehigh
Overall confidencehigh
Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iẓi with nonpast v/pp and past nt/tt, Kannada iẓi/iẓipu and the retained Parji iṛv and Gadaba iṛg independently establish vowel-first order. K03 pp.188–190 compares velar and labial nonpast stems and nasal past formations.

Direction. Agreement between SD I and Central Dravidian supports older i–ẓ. The velar is independently present in Toda, Kannada, Parji and Gadaba formations, so Telugu digu does not require an invented velar inserted after metathesis.

Derivation and relative chronology. K03 p.189 derives *iẓ-g > *ẓi-gg > ḍiggu > ḍigu > digu: displacement, voiced-stop gemination and later degemination. Distinct *iẓ(i)-mpp > ḍimp and *iẓ(i)-ntt > *iẓ(i)-ncc > ḍinc retain old nonpast/past transitive formations. *iẓ-nd > dindu lexicalizes the intransitive past. ẓ > ḍ and later ḍ > d are separate positional developments.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Short i in digu is compatible with a consonantal formative and later degemination; it must not be judged against an invented identical *iẓigV sequence with two vowels. The precise prehistoric suffix paradigm is K03’s reconstruction, not attested Proto-Dravidian. DEDR explicitly labels Gondi forms Telugu loans; K03 p.162 and PSS83 p.234 diagnose Kolami/Naikri borrowing. Naiki extensions remain recipient morphology. Kui d/ḍ transcription differs between Winfield works, noted by DEDR; do not convert that source discrepancy into a dated sound change.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. K03 pp.162,188–190; K61 pp.52–53 §1.124 as cited by K03; PSS83 p.234; DEDR 502

d504 — pull, drag, pant

d504: pull, drag, pant

PropertyAnnotation
Primary familyd504
Comparative input*i/īẓ-u-; long and short formations
Initial consonantØ
V1 quality / quantityi/ī / mixed/uncertain
C2 identity / structureẓ / singleton
Following vowelu
Root/formation shapeVC-u / VVC-C
Grammatical categoryverb
Boundary evidenceShort *iẓ-u and long *īẓ-C formations distinguished; exact inherited quantity conditioning not assumed.
Input classmixed-or-uncertain-quantity
Telugu hypothesisoutside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule
Input confidencemedium
Overall confidencemedium
Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam iẓu, Kannada iẓ/īẓ/eẓe and Konda īṛis independently support a vowel before the apical, but not one invariant original quantity. Telugu īḍucu belongs to the long series; Tamil short iẓu cannot alone fix its exact input.

Direction. Several branches agree on vowel-first order. Kui/Kuvi ḍr- may be innovative under cognacy, but the two-consonant onset cannot be derived by a bare swap with a single reconstructed ẓ without an independent consonant history.

Derivation and relative chronology. Long *īẓ- > Telugu īḍ- with suffix -cu retains order. An independently short *iẓ-k- > *iḍk > igg is a possible medial-assimilation route to iggu; exact cluster details remain conditional. Kui *iẓ-u-p > *ẓip plus ẓ > ḍr, or an earlier local consonant complex, could yield ḍripa; neither is established here. Brahui rūsing may reflect initial-vowel loss from a related u-vowel stem plus its own s extension.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. PSS83 p.244 places Brahui rūs among cases compatible with aphaeresis, not among its two stronger reversal cases. Long vowel controls cannot be defined using only modern Telugu length. Toda īṣf is explicitly alternatively compared with d542 īr; its imported Tamil iẓu cross-reference is not a Toda lexeme. Differences among pull, pant and suck formations may also involve distinct morphology.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 504, including alternative Toda comparison; PSS83 p.244 example 821

Independent input evidence. Tamil iẓai, Kota iṛ- and Kannada eḷasu favor an initial vowel and apical. Telugu/Kannada/Kolami deŋg has a velar nasal expansion; the imported *deŋ does not establish earlier order.

Direction. The non-Telugu vowel-first comparison supports a potential displacement history, but the differing expansions and the source’s queried link to d457 iṇai leave exact cognacy less secure.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *iẓ-aŋk > *eẓaŋk > *ẓēŋk > *ḍēŋg > dẽg requires contraction, ẓ > ḍ > d and shortening/nasal changes. That full suffix input is not independently attested. Kannada deŋgu and Kolami deŋg may reflect Telugu-area diffusion.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Sexual-union vocabulary may spread or undergo expressive restructuring; this is a hypothesis requiring historical distribution, not a reason to exclude a inconvenient form automatically. Do not count Kannada and Kolami as independent innovations or reconstruct their suffix entirely from Telugu.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Malayalam iẓayuka supplies the sole unshifted comparator; Telugu ḍē̃ku/dē̃ku has an additional nasal and velar. The source-level PSTDr label does not prove a wider reconstructed clade.

Direction. The matching meaning and known vowel-first ẓ roots make earlier *iẓ plausible, but an independently shared nasal-velar derivative is missing.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *iẓ-aŋk > *eẓaŋk > *ẓēŋk > ḍē̃ku > dē̃ku; dē̃kuru adds further morphology. Malayalam ēyuka can instead reflect medial ẓ loss and vowel contraction while remaining vowel-initial.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not use Telugu ē alone as independent evidence for low *a. A second unshifted velar formation or early textual cognate would strengthen this etymology; otherwise separate inheritance from diffusion or accidental semantic resemblance.

Independent input evidence. Tamil iḷai/iḷaippu, Malayalam iḷaykkuka and Kannada iḷidu support an initial vowel before lateral. Telugu ēlanna has a different nominal ending.

Direction. All secure comparisons begin with a vowel; Telugu ēl retains V–l and provides no evidence for l-initial displacement.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The low-vowel weary formation is an observed retention, but exact Telugu nn and long ē history needs lexical/historical support. Badaga heḷa explicitly competes with d4419; do not use it to reconstruct original h/c.

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iḷa/iḷam/iḷai, Kannada eḷa/eḷatu and Parji/Gadaba ile/iled independently support vowel-first short root. Exact proto *i versus *e must be separated from the secure relative vowel/lateral order.

Direction. Agreement of SD I and Central Dravidian makes original V–ḷ more likely than independent vowel insertion into a common l-initial root. Telugu ela provides internal retained evidence without being the sole basis.

Derivation and relative chronology. Low-vowel derivatives *iḷ-aŋk > *eḷaŋk > *lēŋk > Telugu lē̃ga and *iḷ-ant > *lēnt > lē̃ta illustrate lowering plus displacement and subsequent nasal/stop changes. Telugu ela retains the root in other formations. Human and calf suffixes have distinct histories; Kui lāvenju/Kuvi lāa may preserve a differently ordered lowering/displacement history if correctly cognate.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. K80’s reassignment of Kui/Kuvi young-person forms to this family partly relies on the proposed rule, so those forms cannot independently prove that same rule. Konda lēta is explicitly a Telugu loan, whereas lēŋa requires a separate inheritance/contact assessment. PSS83 p.234 labels Kolami/Naikri lēŋga borrowed; Naikri lēta has the Telugu form too. Kurux lidum may be a regional loan or another formation. Telugu nelãta adds n while keeping medial l; it is not simple metathesis. Historical ḷēnṟu titles are being separately checked in DHARMA, not treated as modern independent roots.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 513; K80 table 1 item 2 and discussion; PSS83 p.234; DHARMA Telugu 00038/00040 (historical appendix)

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṟai/iṟaŋku/iṟakku, Kannada eṟagu, Kodagu əraŋg and Telugu eṟãgu establish short vowel before the alveolar. The displayed elephant *yĀn-ay is a mislinked reconstruction and is excluded.

Direction. Independent SD I witnesses support older V–ṟ. Telugu port ṟēvu/rēvu is displaced relative to the comparable Malayalam iṟavu valley noun, while Telugu descend/bow preserves the fuller nasal-velar formation.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *iṟ-av > *eṟav > *ṟēv > historical ṟēvu > rēvu; *iṟ-aŋk > eṟãgu retains order. Gondi ray/rey and Konda ṟe/ṟes are shortened/extended displaced stems. Tulu ija beside japp/jāp suggests local initial-vowel loss plus ṟ-related consonant changes; an exact history is not a bare r swap.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The database dates Old Telugu ṟēvu to tenth-century place names; these are source assertions pending inscription-level identification. Pengo jū has an unexplained vowel under a uniform low-a rule. K80 proposes moving some d2456 Kui jāpa/Manda forms here: treat that as a cognacy hypothesis, not an extra certain row. Irula ṟaŋgu may reflect local aphaeresis or contraction and has short/long variants. Toda hair-vow compound is explicitly borrowed from Tamil, distinct from inherited direction/swallow forms.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 516; K80 table 1 item 5 and reassignment discussion; original DEDR historical labels

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṟavu/iṟā and Malayalam iṟāvu support vowel-first alveolar order. Tulu eṭṭi has an additional geminate/consonant history. The prawn reconstructions mislinked to d533 are related scholarly proposals, not fly inputs.

Direction. Southern vowel-first names favor earlier V–ṟ, making Telugu reyya/royya plausibly innovative. Regional rēy nouns could nevertheless have spread after a single change.

Derivation and relative chronology. Possible *iṟ-ay > *eṟay > *ṟēy > reyya with gemination/shortening; royya additionally requires vowel rounding or an independently rounded variant. Tamil -av and eastern -y are not silently assumed identical. Konda ṟeyo preserves distinct alveolar transcription.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The o in royya is not predicted by a uniform *i+a > ē account; contact or rounding needs independent evidence. Gondi Koya and Gadaba reyya are especially close to Telugu and remain contact candidates. Parji rēḍa has a different consonant ending; its inheritance versus regional diffusion needs historical support. No separate root counts for dialect variants.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 517; prawn *eṯ-V-y reconstruction is mislinked under d533 in Jambu

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṟu and Malayalam iṟuka independently establish a high-u formation and vowel-first alveolar. Telugu iriyu differs in final vowel, while Kui renga/repka contains additional consonantal morphology.

Direction. The southern comparison plus Kurux e-initial cognates favors earlier initial vowel. Kui initial r is plausibly displaced but its exact formative vowel is not established from the southern u verb.

Derivation and relative chronology. Telugu *iṟ-i > iriyu retains order. Kui *iṟ-Vŋk > reng and *iṟ-Vk-p > *rekp > repk could reflect initial displacement followed by a morphologically motivated k/p exchange. The first operation’s vowel history is underdetermined; the second is explicitly given in DEDR.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not infer a low formative from Kui e alone. Kurux esnā/eṣ-type consonant development is separate and does not erase the initial vowel. The published underlying rek-p and past rekt provide stronger direction evidence for consonant-cluster metathesis than this set provides for the exact earlier initial vowels.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Kui ṛuhpa may reflect initial loss before a retained u vowel or a separately formed displaced stem.

Telugu iṟi/iṟiyu retain high-i formations too. The complex adversity nouns must not be counted as independent retained roots or assumed fully derived merely from semantic similarity.

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṟai/iṟaivaṉ and Kannada eṟe/eṟeya establish vowel-first low-ay input independently. Telugu historical eṟa is a retained title, while ṟē̃ḍu incorporates a human ending.

Direction. Independent SD I agreement plus historical Telugu eṟa favors older vowel before alveolar. The displaced extended title is not a reason to reclassify the bare historical title as noncognate.

Derivation and relative chronology. *iṟ-ay-anṟu > *eṟayanṟu > *ṟēyanṟu > ṟē̃ḍu is a plausible schematic path; exact y loss and human-ending assimilation require their own chronology. Malayalam iṟān > rān can instead result from aphaeresis.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. DEDR identifies eṟa in a seventh–eighth-century Nellore inscription, citing Master BSOAS 12:351. This date belongs to that source claim pending primary inscription check. The singular/human morphology is independently motivated, but no blanket claim that all human suffixes trigger metathesis follows.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil iṟai/iṟappu, Malayalam iṟa and Kannada eṟake/eṟakil establish initial vowel and low formative; Kodagu ərakɨ corroborates the velar roof formation.

Direction. The southern vowel-first forms make Konda ṟēkam, Kui rēpa and Pengo jēgom likely innovations. Telugu retains eṟa as the second member of a well-parapet compound.

Derivation and relative chronology. Possible *iṟ-ak > *eṟak > *ṟēk > Konda ṟēkam/Pengo jēgom, followed by local consonant/ending changes. Kui rēpa has a labial formation, compared with Tamil iṟappu. Telugu talli-y-eṟa retains the vowel of the second member, with a boundary glide.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This Telugu attestation tests a compound-medial environment, not necessarily the rule’s word-initial domain. It must remain in the dataset but separate from free simplex counterexamples. Badaga topographic names multiply records without multiplying roots; only ere and ere mane are direct lexical witnesses.

PropertyAnnotation

Eligibility / caveatoutside-target-control

Independent input evidence. Tamil ī, Malayalam īcca, Kota īp and Toda īpy support a vowel-only long root with distinct extensions. Telugu ī̃ga has a velar/nasal formation. Prawn *eṯ-V-y under this entry is a mislinked reconstruction.

Direction. There is no reconstructed initial vowel–apical sequence to reverse in the fly simplex. Initial consonants in honey/flower compounds belong to their first members, not a moved segment of ī.

Derivation and relative chronology. Telugu *ī-Nk > ī̃ga retains initial long vowel. Kolami/Naikri nīŋga may add n or preserve a different formation. Tamil tēṉ-ī, Gondi pʰuk+ī, Kui pūk+i and Kurux tīn+ī are compounds, not evidence for original *tēn as the fly root.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The imported *tēn fly/bee reconstruction conflates compound material with the simplex hypothesis unless independently argued. Brahui hīṛ̆ẖ has prothetic/extended consonants requiring its own history. Tulu ippi is strengthened and denotes fly eggs. Latin Bombinatrix glabra is not a Telugu word. These are scope controls, excluded from the apical denominator.

Mechanism scope. No eligible apical in the inherited simplex; compound and extension histories separate.

Independent input evidence. Tamil īcal/īyal, Malayalam īyal and Kannada īcal support a long initial vowel and medial palatal/glide, followed by a lateral suffix. Telugu isuḷḷu/usiḷḷu differs in quantity, vowel quality and lateral strengthening.

Direction. Southern long ī followed by c/y precedes the later lateral, whereas Telugu has short i/u. The two Telugu variants differ in the order of their vowels, not initial promotion of an apical.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *īcal > *ical > *isalu > isuḷḷu requires shortening, palatal weakening, rounding and morphological strengthening; this is not a fully demonstrated chain. isuḷḷu versus usiḷḷu is compatible with vowel-order reversal or assimilatory variation. Singular usiḍi and plural usiḷḷu require a separate ḍ/ḷḷ paradigm.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Do not infer the direction of i/u reversal from which variant is listed first. Earlier Telugu attestations or dialect paradigms could distinguish vowel metathesis from rounding/unrounding. DEDR compares fly d533, so conservative sensitivity may group insect-root formations, without assuming full identity.

Mechanism scope. Possible vowel metathesis or vowel-quality variation; initial-apical rule inapplicable.

Scholarly references. DEDR 536 p.53 directly checked

Independent input evidence. Tamil uka/uva and Kota og support a vowel-first root with velar/labial correspondence. Malayalam uvakka and Telugu uvvāyi support a labial series. Kannada ō is compatible with medial consonant loss.

Direction. Multiple southern witnesses support vowel before k/v, but DEDR explicitly questions the Telugu gōmu comparison. Its initial g does not establish a historical velar swap.

Derivation and relative chronology. Tamil uvakai > ōkai is explicitly contraction after medial consonant loss. A hypothetical *uk-am > *kōm > gōmu would require velar displacement and contraction, but the matching -am formation is not independently supplied by this set.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Keep gōmu uncertain instead of creating an exception to the apical condition from a queried cognate. Telugu uvviḷ-ūru compounds retain initial uv; their additional lateral and light-verb material must not be treated as root consonants. Kannada ose and the Kota lover compounds are also queried in the original source.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil ukā/uvā, Malayalam uka-maram and Telugu uvva support vowel-first tree-name variants. Kannada ogani/uguni beside gōṇi/gōnu supplies internal initial-order variation with a nasal formation.

Direction. Independent vowel-first velar forms favor earlier uk/og in the relevant regional tree-name family; exact cognacy is weakened by several botanical identifications and differing extensions.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional Kannada *og-an > *gōn > gōṇi/gōnu resembles nonapical displacement with contraction. Alternative initial-vowel loss plus lengthening or loan adaptation remains possible. Telugu *uv-a > uvva retains initial order and strengthens the labial.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. A Kannada velar case cannot automatically establish the Telugu apical rule. Careya, Dillenia, Salvadora and Aleurites identifications differ in the original source; botanical-name transfer must be evaluated before asserting one inherited etymon. Latin Careya arborea is not a Malayalam lexeme.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam ukir, Kannada ugur and Tulu uguru establish southern vowel–velar–vowel–rhotic. Telugu/Konda gōru, Central Dravidian gōr and Brahui hōr form another regional set; Kurux orᵒx and Malto orgu have r before velar. K03 p.484 deliberately lists distinct regional reconstructions.

Direction. The broad southern sequence favors *ukir for SD I, but cannot by itself decide whether all gōr and ork forms arose from that exact proto-input. A universal *okar selected to yield gōr would use the outcome to choose the second vowel.

Derivation and relative chronology. Conditional *ok-ar > *ko-ar > kōr > gōru would require exceptional displacement of a velar, contraction and voicing. Alternatively a separate *kōr stem and an expanded southern *ukir need a deeper morphological/phonological explanation. Kurux/Malto could show *ukir > *urk > ork with liquid/velar reversal, but inherited *ork is also possible; direction is not fixed.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This is not evidence that the ordinary Telugu apical condition freely extends to k. The same gōr family spans several subgroups and Brahui, so a late Telugu-only event is insufficient. Kui unguli looks like an Indo-Aryan finger term and must be checked against the original source instead of counted as a conservative ukir reflex. Parji gēri has a separate vowel history. Related d926/d2257 comparisons remain to adjudicate.

Mechanism scope. Competing regional reconstructions; nonapical displacement and internal consonant reversal remain hypotheses.

Scholarly references. DEDR 561; K03 pp.109,484; PSS83 exceptional *okar discussion

Independent input evidence. Tamil uku and Kannada ugu corroborate vowel-first velar root. Tulu ugipu directly supports an expanded transitive formation beside guppuni; Telugu guppu shares the latter consonant-first shape.

Direction. Independent southern vowel-first roots and Tulu ugipu favor an earlier initial vowel in the family. Exact cognacy of the formerly separate guppu entry is a published DEDR merger, not established by shape alone.

Derivation and relative chronology. Possible *uk-upp > *ku-upp > kupp/g upp with contraction, or *ugipp > gipp/gupp by initial loss plus vowel adjustment. Telugu ūcu can reflect a different suffix/cluster development with a surviving initial vowel; it is not the retained exact counterpart of guppu.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The Tulu/ Telugu transitive pair is a serious nonapical comparison, but homogeneous u vowels leave literal exchange versus aphaeresis weakly identifiable. Parji uy/uv can arise through medial velar weakening. A distinct expressive throw verb or contact between Tulu and Telugu remains to rule out; do not settle it by labeling every g-initial form metathesis.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 562 p.55 directly checked; DEN1 merger of old DED 1443 into 480

Direction. All present lexical witnesses are vowel-initial; an earlier apical plus assimilation is a hypothesis needing the separate d708 comparison.

Derivation and relative chronology. Regional *ugg > Telugu uggamu/Kannada ugga involves nominal endings, not initial displacement. Naiki ugur/uggur/ogur shows consonant strength and vowel variation, with a rhotic after the velar.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Tamil ukkam is explicitly a Telugu loan and supplies no independent proto-input. A related Prakrit ukkā well-lever term is cited by DEDR, leaving diffusion direction and scope open. Count as a geminate/control formation, not an independently established singleton apical counterexample.

Independent input evidence. Tamil uṭal/uṭampu, Malayalam uṭal and Kannada oḍal independently support vowel-first retroflex with low second vowel. Konda oṛol and Kota oṛḷ preserve the same consonant order.

Derivation and relative chronology. *uṭ-al > *oḍal > Telugu oḍalu > oḷḷu via medial-vowel loss and retroflex/lateral assimilation. Kannada ḍoḷḷu/doḷḷu and Tulu ḍoḷḷu/ṭoḷḷu could involve aphaeresis/displacement plus expressive strengthening, but may instead be separately expressive belly words.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The independently matched low-a body noun is a substantive Telugu retained-order case. The southern consonant-initial potbelly forms should not be counted as inherited metathesis until their derivation or early attestations are established. Toda v before its reflex is prothesis, not movement of the medial retroflex. Badaga bodily cloth compounds do not create new root evidence.

Mechanism scope. Telugu medial assimilation; southern initial-loss/expressive alternatives unresolved.

Independent input evidence. Tamil uṭu/uṭuppu, Malayalam uṭuppu and Kannada uḍu/uḍupu independently support matching u vowels and a labial clothing formation. Telugu uḍupu directly matches this series.

Direction. SD I and Konda/Gondi/Pengo/Manda vowel-first forms agree; no initial apical promotion is necessary even where medial vowels or consonants are lost.

Derivation and relative chronology. *uṭ-upp > Telugu uḍupu through voicing/lenition, retaining order. Syncope gives Konda uRpa and Pengo uspa; local apical weakening gives Manda uhpa. These histories remove/alter the medial consonant while leaving the initial vowel.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Same-vowel u+u is not sufficient to trigger contraction/displacement: this is a direct counterexample to application of such a blanket rule. Indo-Aryan *ōḍḍh clothing words are linked contact comparisons and do not determine the Dravidian reconstruction. Toda non-Toda dress noun may reflect cultural diffusion and does not add a separate root.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 587; DEN1 p.401 additions; linked CDIAL 2547 kept separate

Independent input evidence. Telugu uḍuku/uḍikincu, Gondi uḍk ēru and Kuvi uḍku show vowel-first retroflex-plus-velar heat words; Kurux uṛturnā supports a related vowel-first root with a different extension.

Direction. The available roots all retain V–apical order. Gondi/Kuvi may have borrowed the Telugu regional heat word, so they do not independently prove its high second vowel.

Derivation and relative chronology. Telugu *uḍ-uk > uḍuku; syncope produces uḍk in hot-water compounds. Kurux *uṭ-t > uṛt is a separate derivative/correspondence hypothesis, not a displaced form.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The apparent Tamil udku is actually Keikadi quoted by Hislop and explicitly < Telugu. Keikadi has no resolved research language mapping here; preserve the source observation separately rather than count it as inherited Tamil. Bibliographic fragments parsed as Tamil are excluded.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Derivation and relative chronology. Regional uḍutV > uḍute/uḍuta through final-vowel variation, retaining order.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Two-language distribution permits lexical diffusion. A broader squirrel comparison is needed before asserting Proto-Dravidian antiquity or using this as a decisive inherited exception. Do not manufacture gemination or a low vowel to explain its retention.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 590, compare d713

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam uṭumpu, Kodagu uḍumbɨ and Telugu uḍumu directly support a u-vowel labial-nasal animal name. Central Dravidian uḍug/uṛug has a distinct velar expansion.

Direction. Widespread vowel-first names, including Gondi/Konda, support older u–ṭ order independent of Telugu.

Derivation and relative chronology. *uṭ-ump > Telugu uḍumu involves medial voicing and loss/assimilation of the labial stop after m, without initial displacement. Konda uṟbu and Gondi urpal involve syncope and apical/labial changes; Kolami uḍug is a different suffix formation.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Another same-vowel u+u retention in an independently matched inherited-looking formation. Source identifications include monitor, pangolin and anteater; DEDR itself questions one pangolin meaning. Those zoological uncertainties may affect individual cognacy but cannot erase the stable southern monitor comparison. Naikri h is prothetic; Irula i/u differs while order is retained.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil uṭai/uṭaimai/uṭaiyāṉ, Malayalam uṭaya/uṭama, Kannada oḍeya/oḍame and Telugu oḍami/oḍayãḍu independently support the low-ay possession formation.

Direction. Several southern languages agree in initial vowel before retroflex; Telugu owner nouns preserve this sequence even with a human ending comparable in function to displaced lord d527.

Derivation and relative chronology. *uṭ-ay > *oḍay through lowering before a, followed by nominal/human suffixes, gives Telugu oḍayãḍu/oḍayũḍu without initial displacement. *uṭ-am > oḍami/oḍame gives property nouns. Kota oyṛm may reflect glide/apical reordering locally; this does not move the apical before the first vowel.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. This directly limits a claim that low-a or human morphology alone determines Telugu application. Kurux ūṇḍrī/ū̃ṛī requires nasal and suffix history and is less secure as the exact same formation. Old Marathi oḍēra is a contact comparison, not evidence for Proto-Dravidian order. Homophonous wear uṭu d587 may be historically related but is not automatically merged.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil urai/ura, Malayalam ura/urekka and Kannada ore establish a low-vowel speech formation; Parji ur groan independently preserves vowel-first root order.

Direction. The independent southern and central comparison supports older u–r; Telugu uraka retains that order alongside rō̃ju/rō̃juḍu.

Derivation and relative chronology. Possible *ur-añc > *orañc > *rōñc > rō̃ju requires a nasal-palatal formative not fully matched here. Telugu uraka/ūraka is source-analyzed as a negative gerund and retains the initial vowel; its length is not evidence for displacement. roda has an additional dental and may have a separate expressive or contact history.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Negative morphology could contribute to retention, but a single family does not establish a rule that negation blocks metathesis. Gondi ronjānā may share the derived stem or borrow it. Codagu answer has an explicit alternative comparison with d650; the noisy/expressive series cannot be unified just by broad speech semantics.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Independent input evidence. Tamil ura/uram/uravu, Malayalam uram and Kannada urku/oraṭu establish a vowel-first strength root. Kannada urku beside ukku independently shows the medial cluster potentially underlying Telugu ukku.

Direction. The full southern forms and Kannada urku support r after u, with later loss/assimilation in ukku; they do not require r ever to have moved to word onset.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ur-k > *ukk > Telugu ukku, with a velar expansion and assimilation/loss of r. Kannada oraṭu > orṭu/uṭṭu supplies a parallel dental-cluster development. Toda pith ūṇ requires different nominal/nasal history.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu ukku hides the root rhotic, but its retained initial vowel favors medial assimilation over a concealed initial metathesis. The homophonous steel word d661 has a related heat/melting analysis; merge these only as a sensitivity scenario, not an established etymology of strength from steel.

Mechanism scope. Medial cluster assimilation; no initial displacement.

Independent input evidence. Tamil/Malayalam ural and Kannada oral/oraḷ independently support short u/o before r and low a after it. Tulu oralɯ/uraḷɯ supplies a fourth southern comparison.

Direction. Independent agreement supports earlier vowel-first ural, making Telugu rōlu a strong displacement-family case. The displayed *uram-kkal grinding-stone compound is not silently substituted for the simpler mortar noun.

Derivation and relative chronology. *ur-al > *or-al > *rōl > Telugu rōlu. Literal *roual contraction versus lowering/assimilation followed by initial-vowel loss is not uniquely recoverable. Kannada oral > orḷu > oḷḷu instead loses/assimilates the medial rhotic and retains the initial vowel. Kota oḷkāl contains stone-compound morphology.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Telugu ṟōlu versus rōlu has an alveolar/rhotic transcription issue: original non-Telugu ural supports r, and a separate Telugu r/ṟ history is required. Do not use the later spelling to reconstruct original *ṟ. The d665 rub comparison may make this a derivative of the same root; family sensitivity must collapse mortar and rubbing when assessing independence.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 651; PSS83 p.234 example 780; K61 vowel-initial section

Independent input evidence. Malayalam uṟi, Kannada uril/urul and Telugu uri/urulu preserve vowel-first order; exact original r/ṟ and formative i/u vary in the comparison.

Direction. Southern and Konda/Kuvi vowel-first forms favor older u–rhotic, while Kui ruhu/rusu probably lost the initial vowel or displaced the rhotic in a separately extended stem.

Derivation and relative chronology. Telugu uri retains order; urulu/uralu adds a lateral extension. A possible *ur-c > ucc underlies uccu, but this extension is not directly reconstructed from the noose noun alone. Kui *uru-s > ru-s can be aphaeresis; homogeneous vowels cannot independently show exchange. Kuvi huru adds an initial h before the retained u–r sequence.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. Kuvi short, long and strengthened-r variants are separate dialect/source observations, not separate roots. Konda ūri lengthens without metathesis. Possible d582 linkage noted by DEDR may alter the deeper analysis; retain uncertainty rather than count uccu as proof of an original palatal.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Eligibility / caveatcore

Independent input evidence. Tamil uru/uruppu/urumam, Kannada uripu/urupu, Tulu uri and Central Dravidian urj establish a vowel-first heat root. Its formatives independently vary between i and u.

Direction. Agreement of southern and central branches favors earlier u–r; eastern rū/rund stems are innovative under cognacy. Telugu uriyu and uralu retain the original order.

Derivation and relative chronology. A same-u formation *ur-u > *rū can yield Konda rūṇ(u), Kuvi rūh and Pengo rūmi/rūc with further suffixes; shorter Kui ru/rut and Manda rund need distinct cluster/quantity histories. Telugu ummalincu may continue *ur-m with medial assimilation, not initial displacement.

Exceptions and discriminating evidence. The exact suffix of Konda summer sweat and Pengo sweat is not recoverable from a generic burn root alone. Hume’s earlier VLV > LV example is therefore a family-level generalization, not proof that every *uri derivative moved. Brahui hushing may involve prothesis and consonant change but the r history is unclear. Toda yry contains a vowel represented y, not an initial palatal consonant.

Mechanism scope. Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

Scholarly references. DEDR 656; Hume 2004 p.226 VLV > LV discussion
